mr. chairman, please! europe can of course play a huge role in the long-running global warming process, but only if self-discipline, solidarity and truth prevail over the vagueness of the law and the fraud and manipulation of emissions trading. while it is true that the kyoto protocol is an international achievement that committed industrialized countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, the negotiated scope of emission reductions is a political compromise. it does not reflect the assumptions of scientists who calculate that 60% of carbon dioxide is needed to halt climate change, not 5% or 8%, which is something the union is proud of and which has also been achieved at the expense of countries where, unfortunately, the preaccession preparations have led to the destruction of industry. land use change (forestry) is also being used as an instrument of the kyoto protocol's climate policy. after all, there's really no reliable way of knowing how much carbon is being sequestered by trees - it's a process. this is why some afforestation plans under the so-called "clean development mechanism" are controversial. of course they deserve attention, but from our polish point of view we oppose the prospect of poland becoming a forest where the rich elite are going to travel to hunt. the burden of mitigating climate change should be shared equally across national responsibilities. rich, developed, highly industrialized countries have benefited enormously from developing countries and are responsible for a huge amount of environmental destruction, but they are much less willing to take financial responsibility, whether it's the united states or the european union. many also wonder whether the kyoto commitments are more of a hindrance than an aid to accelerating change. despite these shortcomings, we recognise the usefulness of the entry into force of the agreements, with the understanding that more stringent commitments to reduce emissions should be made.
mr. speaker, the house! climate change is a natural fact: there are warmer periods and colder periods. does human activity have any bearing on this? i have serious doubts. experts debate the issue, and there is no conclusive evidence. there is no doubt that the increase in carbon dioxide in the air has a positive effect on crop production and that the excess carbon in the atmosphere is effectively absorbed by the biosphere: forests, humus, sea, etc. on the other hand, there is no doubt that co2 emissions from industrial combustion processes are always accompanied by emissions of other gases that are clearly harmful to the environment: forests, agricultural production, architectural monuments and, above all, human health. so it is worthwhile to appreciate all the efforts that have been made to promote technologies that reduce the burning of fossil fuels. as the negative consequences of incineration are transboundary, the costs must also be spread across international agreements. the kyoto protocol logically shifts the cost of reducing emissions from countries that have made the effort to countries that are not doing enough. climate change has been and will be, and we have little control over it, but anthropogenic emissions into the atmosphere are a problem that humanity must address through collective effort. this collective effort deserves our full support. the shift towards renewable energy and energy-efficient technologies is particularly welcome. it costs money. without international solidarity, there will be no progress in this regard. but let's not be fooled into thinking that every natural disaster, every storm or flood, drought or tsunami, is caused by greenhouse gas emissions. let's just walk the earth and stick to the facts. thank you, sir.
mr president, this session of the european parliament is historic. we have been presented with a draft resolution on the treaty establishing a constitution for europe, and by adopting this resolution our parliament - launched this process with a first step, which was the single act, negotiated under the luxembourg presidency. i would also like to say to those who have attacked and criticized this draft constitution that, of course, in a democratic debate, we respect their position. but it is not with 19th century speeches that we offer a perspective to the people of today, not only europeans, but also the world of the 21st century. the answer in a globalised world is not to retreat into the past and return to outdated sovereignty schemes. they offer no solution for prosperity, democracy and peace, neither to europeans nor to others. i would also like to say to those who make a subtle distinction between a non-pro-european and an anti-european, that it is a no, because the rejection of the constitution is simply a defeat of europe, a defeat of a more open, more transparent, more democratic europe, offering prospects both inside and outside, a stronger europe. so i think we should not get lost in such subtleties. of course, as the rapporteur has said, not everything in this constitution is perfect. we all wish we had made some improvements. but is not the essence of democracy, in a certain sense, imperfection, since democracy lives on compromise and, therefore, we must be able to accept a compromise of progress today, in order to go further tomorrow? the constitution provides a solid foundation for our common values, as has been said by several speakers. it provides a democratic framework for the european union to act more effectively where action is needed under the principle of subsidiarity. the union's motto, 'united in diversity', is, as has been said, the essence of this europe. the balance between large and small member states, equality between citizens, respect for national identities, which has been stressed by many, is the very essence of our union, which is very well reflected in this constitutional text. there's been some progress. maybe they're not enough. we would have liked to go further on the jha or the foreign policy side, but i think this is a very important first step. nor should we now consider revising it. of course, every constitution must provide for revision mechanisms, as this one does; it also provides for different types of work. the improvements will come over the years, provided that this constitution is adopted, that we are able to apply it and build a genuine european democracy through it. this text was drawn up with the wide participation not only of national and european parliamentarians and representatives of the member states, but also of representatives of civil society. there has been a debate, albeit insufficient, in civil society. this debate must be encouraged and supported, participatory democracy is an innovative fact, so much so that it is hardly found in our national constitutions. it is a matter of bringing it to life and giving it a concrete content. the debate on vice-president of thecommission. mr president, i would like to thank you all for this long but stimulating debate. the vast majority of the comments have rightly paid tribute to this excellent report and to the work of the co-rapporteurs. hopefully, it will receive the overwhelming support of this house tomorrow. i am conscious that this report and the constitution need to be put into historical perspective. this is the first time that the european parliament has not had a list of regrets about the result of an intergovernmental conference, and we can ask one of the veterans in this kind of work about this. if i compare this report to the planas, méndez de vigo and tsatsos reports, for example, it is the most positive assessment of the outcome of an intergovernmental conference. i share the views of those calling for a wide and honest debate. without debate we do not have a democracy and, without debate, we do not get closer to the truth. it is therefore our responsibility to provide examples of how the constitution will affect the daily lives of european citizens. the word 'perfect' has been mentioned. i have been a commissioner for only five years and i have not yet seen the 'perfect' document. if you look around, how could we find a perfect document? commission. mr president, your debate today on the issue of the earthquake and tsunami in south-east asia shows the commitment of the european parliament to see action by the european union to help the countries and populations in need. i can assure you that the commission will deliver the help that is needed and will do this in close cooperation with you. i thank you for a number of useful comments and suggestions in this respect. as regards the reaction of the commission's civil protection unit, it immediately organised the sending of member state experts to the affected countries – the first experts arrived the day after the disaster. what are the concrete measures to be taken? as the president of the commission underlined, there are a number of proposals to be implemented, some of them in the short term, others in the mid- and long-term. on the humanitarian side, in addition to the support package already adopted, it is proposed that eur 100 million from the commission's jakarta pledge be allocated from the emergency reserve. i understand that the budgetary authority has already agreed to this politically. on the reconstruction side, some eur 350 million of partially new funds should be made available, and funds already programmed streamlined. i have noted your concerns about the reprogramming, but i should like to assure you that this improved streamlining of all the available funds is the quickest way to deliver aid and, in many cases, will be necessary, as some projects cannot be carried out in some of the affected areas. there is a proverb in my country: one who gives fast gives twice. it is important that we bear that in mind. not only are the amounts of aid important; commission. mr president, it is an honour and pleasure for me to present the commission's view on the presidential elections in ukraine. more than seven weeks have now passed since what is commonly described as ukraine's orange revolution. the events during that period have shown that the people of ukraine are committed to democracy and also that the eu member states, by acting together, can play an important role. let me turn now to three questions. first, how far has ukraine come since the first running of the second round of the elections on 21 november 2004, and what does this mean for the country in the future? second, what role has the eu played to assist ukraine to find a peaceful solution to the crisis? third, what are the challenges now in european union-ukraine relations? i shall begin with the developments in ukraine and what they mean for the future. most importantly, ukraine has succeeded in finding a peaceful solution to the crisis it faced after the serious shortcomings in the conduct of the presidential elections and, notably, the first run of the second round on 21 november. the situation posed a threat to the country's legal framework and its territorial integrity, but both of these were preserved. the international election observation mission, led by the osce office for democratic institutions and human rights, found that the re-run of the second round of the presidential elections on 26 december brought ukraine closer to international standards. that is a positive sign. the political compromise reached on 8 december 2004 was important in that it paved the way for a new second round of the presidential elections. it is our firm hope that the compromise will also help promote further democratisation in ukraine. important constitutional changes were agreed, establishing the framework for the country's internal development in the years ahead, and the role of ukraine's parliament has been strengthened. recent events have demonstrated the ukrainian people's strong attachment to democracy. we very much welcome this development. further efforts will be needed to build on this and to take the democratisation process forward in the years ahead. we very much hope that the conduct of the parliamentary elections next year will reflect further progress towards democratisation. now the second question: how has the eu helped ukraine to find a peaceful solution? the eu has given sustained political support to help the people of ukraine find a peaceful outcome to the crisis. it spoke with one voice, urging the ukrainian authorities to show restraint and all parties to express themselves exclusively by non-violent means. the eu also helped to prepare the ground for the political compromise of 8 december 2004, with european mediators, including high representative mr solana, polish president, mr kwasniewski, and the lithuanian president, mr adamkus, playing a very useful facilitating role. the european union also made a major contribution, together with the broader international community, to help ensure that the re-run of the second round of the elections would be fair and free. in concrete terms, the eu sent 587 short-term election observers from the eu member states for the elections on 26 december. the participation in the election observation of a team of nine members of the european parliament, led by mr siwiec, was an important contribution. the european commission financed the participation of a further 150 short-term observers from the non-eu osce member states, as well as voter education activities. overall, the eu played a highly significant role in helping secure correct conduct of the elections on 26 december. finally, what are the challenges ahead in european union-ukraine relations? clearly, now is the time to take a fresh look at our relationship with ukraine as a key neighbour and partner of the european union. through the developments of the past weeks the people of ukraine have already clearly demonstrated their commitment to the development of ukraine into a society that fully respects democracy and fundamental freedoms. however, this is only the beginning of a long process which will require our continued support. the question of ukraine entering the european union is not on the agenda. the european neighbourhood policy is distinct from membership. it will allow us to shift to a higher gear in cooperation with ukraine. within the framework of the european union-ukraine partnership and cooperation agreement, it opens new partnership and economic integration and cooperation perspectives and offers significant upgrading in our relationships. the key tool for putting this into practice is the action plan. last december, the council endorsed the eu-ukraine enp action plan and agreed to forward it to the european union-ukraine cooperation council 'as soon as developments in ukraine allowed'. we all believe that the time has come to move ahead with this action plan. it identifies key priorities such as further strengthening the stability and effectiveness of the institutions, guaranteeing democracy and the rule of law, ensuring the democratic conduct of elections in ukraine in accordance with osce standards, and ensuring respect for the freedom of the media and freedom of expression. it also provides a comprehensive programme for our work with ukraine in all areas of cooperation, with actions identified in the fields of political dialogue, justice and home affairs, economic and trade relations, people-to-people contacts, cross-border activities and shared responsibility in conflict prevention and conflict resolution. we hope that the eu-ukraine cooperation council meeting on 21 february will endorse this action plan, thereby paving the way for ukraine and us to begin work on its implementation. at the council's request, the high representative and the commissioner are working on concrete proposals to strengthen cooperation with ukraine making full use of the action plan, thus enhancing ukraine's relationship with the european union. from the commission's point of view, this proposal should, as far as possible, also take into account ukraine's requests. the commission is convinced that the european neighbourhood policy action plan is a sufficiently comprehensive and flexible tool to allow us to respond to the new situation. the offer the eu makes in the action plan can be modulated to reflect the progress made by the partner. the further a partner is ready to go in taking practical steps to implement common values, the further the eu will be ready to go in strengthening our mutual links. the pace of progress in the enp will thus depend on the pace of progress made by the new ukrainian administration. there is therefore no need to renegotiate the action plan with that administration. the eu has repeatedly acknowledged ukraine's european aspirations and welcomed ukraine's european choice. recent dramatic events in ukraine have reconfirmed the country's place on the european map. we have no doubt that these events will enter into history as a milestone, not only for ukraine but also for the eu's relations with that country. the european union and ukraine have a common interest in further reinforcing their political, economic and cultural ties. if ukraine fully respects its commitments, as expressed in the action plan, the commission is willing to help ensure that the european neighbourhood policy results in significantly enhanced relations between the european union and ukraine. we trust that the european parliament will support us in all these efforts.

mr president, the objective of the european union in the field of criminal law, as already set out in the tempere programme and later in the hague programme, is to achieve mutual recognition of judgments in criminal matters. this requires good judicial cooperation based on mutual trust. the lack of such cooperation leads to the avoidance of criminal responsibility, to the escape from criminal responsibility in another country and thus also to the increase of the sense of impunity, which results in an increase in crime in europe. that is why my political group welcomes the report by antonio costa, which contains recommendations to the european commission on the creation of a justice quality card. the fundamental rights of the accused, victims and defenders contained in the proposed charter can also be used as criteria for the mutual evaluation of the quality of justice. and although the specific legal basis for this assessment is only to be found in the constitutional treaty, which is not yet binding, it seems that the general basis can already be found in the maastricht treaty. therefore, i believe that the european commission should, in line with the recommendations of the report, start to develop criteria and methodologies for carrying out such an assessment. this is not easy, in particular because account must be taken of the different legal systems based on different legal traditions and cultures and the different systems of judicial organisation in the member states. the methodology for carrying out such an assessment should also lead to reliable and well-analysed conclusions. it should be added that the mutual evaluation of the judiciary should also be complemented by other actions, such as the need not only to respect but also to strengthen the independence and impartiality of the courts from political influence. thank you, sir.

mr president, the proposed changes to the stability and growth pact aim to make fiscal rules more flexible and effective within the european union, but without compromising the fundamental principle of budgetary discipline. i think that these changes are going in the right direction and i would like to draw attention to three things in this context. firstly, the commission's proposals focus mainly on the level of the current budget deficit, while the level of public debt is of secondary importance in these proposals. i think it should be the other way around, because the key to long-term financial stability is the debt-to-gdp ratio, not the deficit ratio in a given year. the deficit ceiling for very highly indebted countries should therefore be more stringent than the deficit ceiling for low-indebted countries. the latter can afford to run higher deficits temporarily because they cannot be punished for behaving properly in the past. the current account deficit criterion should therefore be secondary to the debt criterion. secondly, the way the deficit is calculated must take account of the specific situation in some new member states which have undertaken a difficult reform of their pension systems. in these countries, the expenditure associated with this reform is temporarily increasing because of the need to finance current pensions and to create pension capital for future generations at the same time. these expenditures should not be included in current public expenditure for the purposes of the stability and growth pact, as they do not increase current demand but are part of national savings. new member states cannot be punished for undertaking difficult structural reforms. thirdly, when establishing the principle for calculating the deficit for the purposes of the stability and growth pact, i propose, commissioner, that we consider excluding expenditure relating to payments to the union budget. while such expenditure increases the level of demand across the union, it serves to implement an important principle of solidarity. adopting this solution could facilitate a compromise on the level of the european union budget for 2007-13. i would remind you that some member states are demanding a so-called 'small budget' precisely because they are net contributors to the budget. thank you very much. thank you.
member of the commission. mr president, i thank all the members who have contributed to the debate, which i found extremely interesting. in conclusion, i would like to reiterate the commission's diagnosis. sometimes, in the course of the debate, the commission is attributed ideas which neither it nor i take for granted. the commission and i believe that the main challenge to increasing growth in the european union and the euro area is to increase the growth potential. this requires structural reforms such as those put forward by the commission in its communication on the review and revitalization of the lisbon strategy. if we do not increase the growth potential, the medium and long-term sustainability of our economy, of our model of society, will not be possible and budgetary stability and macroeconomic stability in the short term will be seriously damaged by the lack of growth. that is the diagnosis, and from that point of view, macroeconomic policy, as the kok report says - and i fully agree with that - must support a strategy of structural reforms which increases the growth potential to sustain that growth and to prevent the lack of liquidity, financing and demand from jeopardizing the exploitation of all the growth possibilities which we have achieved thanks to the reforms. the commission considers it a priority to succeed in revitalizing the lisbon strategy and to this end we have put ten priorities on the table and have considered how to improve the capacity to put the lisbon strategy into practice in the reality of each of the member states, in order to achieve, in all of them and in the european union, the objectives we share. objectives which have not been reduced in the commission's communication, but which have been confirmed as they were defined five years ago. as regards the stability pact, mr president, i would like to make a few clarifications. i think it is appropriate that we should have an understanding of what is happening in these weeks, when the council, with the support of the commission through excellent cooperation with the luxembourg presidency, is trying to reach agreement on how to improve the way in which our budgetary discipline mechanisms are implemented in practice and to make the objectives pursued by the treaty, by defining budgetary stability as one of the conditions for economic and monetary union, a more positive and visible reality than the present one. what are we doing? firstly, we reiterate our firm, clear and unambiguous commitment to the reference values set out in the treaty. the 3% is in the treaty and the commission will not allow a reference value in the treaty to be disregarded. i would like to make it clear again, and i will make it clear again as often as necessary, that neither the commission's proposal nor the present unanimous position of all the ecofin ministers is proposing to exclude any category of expenditure from the deficit calculation. what is being asked, in the terms of article 104 of the treaty, is what relevant factors need to be taken into account when analysing why the excessive deficit has occurred or what needs to be done to restore a balanced situation, sustainability of public finances, reducing the level of the deficit below the reference value. we can distinguish, and we are doing so precisely in the debate, between not excluding any category of expenditure and, at the same time, taking into account economic factors, the composition of public expenditure, the state of the cycle, structural reforms under way, in order to see how the preventive part of the pact is being applied, how public finances are in balance in the medium and long term or, in the part of the excessive deficit procedure, what recommendations are really effective for a country in an excessive deficit to regain budgetary balance. to this end, it is extremely important, and this is the second key element in our discussion, to avoid procyclical policies in the implementation of the pact, both in the preventive and in the corrective part of the excessive deficit procedure. one of the most obvious reasons why some countries have broken the 3% deficit rule is that, when they were in the prime of their economic cycle, they did not apply procyclical policies, they did not sufficiently consolidate their public finances, and there are instruments in the treaty such as early warnings, which the constitution also reinforces and attributes directly to the commission, which must be used more effectively. in addition, in each of the member states, national rules must be established to supplement the pressure, the peer pressure, on those who decide at national level the composition of budget revenue and expenditure and therefore the budget deficit of each of the member states, which, i recall, remains a national competence, although, as mrs berès said, the overall result of these national decisions on budgetary policy is a matter of common interest, because we are in an economic and monetary union. as regards the excessive deficit procedure, we are discussing, and this is the most difficult point of our discussion, how the excessive deficit procedure should be launched. i repeat the position, there is no exclusion in expenditure when calculating what the deficit level is. but if you read article 104 of the treaty again, you will see that once the european commission has informed the council that a given country is, in its view, in an excessive deficit situation, the council has full powers, after an overall assessment, an overall assessment article 104 (6) of the treaty to decide 'whether an excessive deficit exists'. we are trying to make sure that the criteria used by the commission when it tells the council that a country is in an excessive deficit coincide with those which the council then considers, so that shocks like those which have occurred in the past do not happen again. so that in respecting the commission's tasks and powers - and the commission will not renounce any of the powers conferred on it by the treaty - and in using the council's tasks and powers - which will also not renounce those conferred on it by the treaty - there are no blocks in this interrelation, in this cooperation, which paralyse the procedure and give rise to conflicts such as those which took place just over a year ago. governance is very important, it is very important that there are national rules to complement the effort by the member states to adopt common rules of budgetary discipline. it is very important, as we have recently seen, to have clear, reliable and secure statistics. the cooperation between the two institutions, the council and the commission, is very important, and the support and debate in parliament, such as is taking place today and which will no doubt take place in the future, is extremely important. it's very important that we come to an agreement. the credibility of economic and monetary union and, in particular, of our single currency in the eyes of the markets has been discussed, and i share this concern. the markets will not understand that truly global scale, even if difficulties sometimes arise. it is therefore clear that the european union must work to improve the functioning of this committee. we must play an active role in its reform, in its functioning, and i think that in the context of reform of the united nations and of the multilateral system in general, this is an extremely important point. we also know that the management of human rights issues in different countries is sometimes part of a long process. we cannot achieve quick results, so we need to diversify our approaches, working on different tables. i approach to this aspect of human rights, and we do not make this aspect a secondary priority, as some have said. i believe we want to play an important role and take a more comprehensive approach to the next item is the debate on the report (a6-0038/2005) by mr ingo schmitt, on behalf of the committee on transport and tourism, on the draft directive of the european parliament and of the council on a community air traffic controller licence (com ((2004) 0473 - c6-0076/2004 - 2004/0146 (co (())).
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, members of the house, members of the commission! the issues raised by the directive of the european parliament and of the council on the community air traffic controller licence are among the most important in the field of civil aviation safety. where the problem is one of potential danger to human life and health, neither non-violence nor arbitrary procedures and actions can be allowed. in this context, i consider the directive to be necessary, indeed essential. the treatment of our airspace as a single european airspace requires precise, unambiguous legislation also for the licensing of air traffic controllers. the work of these people must be carried out with the highest of responsibilities and professionalism. this is a question of professional preparation for work under normal conditions (as if they always occurred) and in emergency situations that may arise. an air traffic controller must therefore be a man of great theoretical knowledge and great practical skill. it must be a person in full physical and mental health (hence the need for time-based checks), a person who is self-controlled and able to cope with emergencies - accidents and terrorism, as my predecessors have said. language skills: of course, a very good command of english as a common language, but also, and especially in relation to potential crisis situations, a knowledge of the local language. i believe that there needs to be a kind of feedback loop in these rules, i.e. systematic verification of the legal effects and possible introduction of the necessary adjustments, especially in the context of further development of electronic and digital technology. in conclusion, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr ingo schmidt, for his efforts in this area. i say this with appreciation as a person who has contributed to the training of polish civil aviation pilots. until recently, i did this while working at rzeszów university of technology. i would also like to see eu law on this important issue adopted and respected outside the european union. the airspace knows no artificial boundaries, and the laws of aeromechanics apply everywhere. so the rules of aviation safety should be universal. perhaps the european union can help. thank you very much. thank you.
the commission's vice-president mr president, the commission is looking forward with confidence to the position of parliament on this matter and i would like to thank all the speakers who have all highlighted the excellent work done by parliament and paid tribute to the rapporteur, mr schmitt. i think this report is very encouraging and i would like to join in the praise and thanks to the rapporteur from the committee on transport and tourism. i now have to give my opinion on the amendments. i will not go through them one by one, mr president. with your permission, i'll be doing some grouping instead. most of the amendments are aimed at clarifying the text of the proposal for a directive and at emphasizing safety, because safety is really the top priority of this text, or at introducing continuing training in the field of safety. this is the case with amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 15. the commission can therefore accept all these amendments. the same applies to amendment no 16, which makes the conditions for the introduction of national indications more restrictive, and to amendment no 18, which aims to simplify the administrative burden. the commission will be able to support your position on the language arrangements, which balance legitimate security concerns with the rights of free movement of controllers; your amendments nos 10 and 17 bring parliament's and the council's positions into genuine agreement. some other amendments are acceptable in principle, provided that their wording is somewhat modified. the commission fully supports the principle of amendment no 6 concerning the monitoring, involvement and consultation of the social partners. i have already stressed this in my first speech. as regards amendment no 14, the commission accepts the idea of increased training in the field of security, but considers that this element has more of a place in annex i, which specifies the content of training. the second amendment introduces the reference to the right to work in the event of mobility. i fully understand the logic behind amendment no 20. the legal basis for such a proposal is, however, safety, an objective pursued through the establishment of standards for the essential safety requirements. i would like to say, as mr savary has said, that there is already community law on this subject. the directive on the posting of workers provides that the conditions of the workplace apply in the case of posting. the commission would therefore be prepared to accept, instead of an article which is not the subject of the text, a recital which explicitly refers, as you requested, to the relevant community law. confirming, as i have just said, the importance of involving the social partners in the implementation and monitoring of this directive, particularly by supporting amendment no 6, i propose to include such a reference to the applicable social law in a recital. in other words, this text, which is essentially focused on security, is set in the context of community social law, which should be recalled in the recitals. there are three amendments which the commission is not in a position to support, mainly for formal reasons. firstly, the commission is of the opinion that there is no need to maintain the requirement of accounting in accordance with international standards, as requested by amendment no 19. continuing training providers, i.e. providers of air traffic control services, are already covered by other community regulations and for small training providers such a requirement seems excessive to us. the commission can therefore accept a complete deletion of the relevant paragraph, since your concern for good management is already covered by other sources of community legislation. on amendment no 21 concerning the wording of the sanctions, the commission prefers to keep the standard formula as it is in fact set out in the general guideline adopted by the council. there is also amendment no 4 which deals with a very important aspect of the introduction of a licence: what to do with holders of a national licence? we do not think that the solution is to postpone the introduction of the new harmonised standards and to have two parallel standards of competence coexist. it would be bad for security. that is why the commission cannot support this amendment. however, it is open to any solution which would favour the rapid introduction of the standards of competence while, of course, respecting the obligations imposed by legal certainty on current licence holders. amendment no 22 was tabled just before the plenary session. as i have said before, the commission supports the consultation and involvement of the social partners, which is essential. more specifically, however, it does not consider that the imposition of such an obligation should necessarily be included in the text. that, ladies and gentlemen, is the commission's general agreement with your work. the commission is indeed in a position to support mr ingo schmitt's report fully and i would add that the positions of the commission and parliament are really very close. the constructive nature of mr ingo schmitt's report is to be emphasized and - i believe it was mr rack who said this earlier - if the original proposal was good, the text is even better. the text is even better, proving once again the value of parliament's role as a co-legislator. so if you support this approach in tomorrow's vote, i believe we will have made progress towards the objectives we all set ourselves: namely, the search for even greater safety in the field of air traffic control. this is what the european citizens expect from us, and this is all the more necessary if we want air traffic to develop in the direction of a very good quality of service, including a level of safety that should make european skies probably the safest skies in the world.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on tuesday at 12 noon.

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i would like to thank the honourable members who have just started a debate on the follow-up to the beijing action programme and its evaluation ten years after its launch. as you know, this issue is currently being discussed at the 49th session of the united nations commission on the status of women. the presidency has already delivered a message, i hope, which gives an overview of the union's commitment to the full and effective implementation of the beijing declaration on action. however, as the work of the session is still in progress, i am not yet in a position to report on the results. today, the european union considers equality between women and men to be a fundamental principle and considers the rights of women and girls to be an inalienable, integral and indivisible part of the universal rights of the human person. the beijing + 10 review is an important moment as it not only allows the union to strengthen its programme and its commitment to the objectives of the beijing action programme, but also provides an opportunity to examine which areas have made progress and where concerted action still needs to be strengthened. the recently published report on progress in the european union under the 'beijing + 10' framework, which was drawn up by the luxembourg presidency, clearly sets out the main results achieved at the level of the eu institutions, as well as the progress made in terms of institutional mechanisms in the member states. however, the presidency's report also identifies the challenges that remain to be met, and mrs gröner has just mentioned some of them in relation to the 12 sensitive areas identified at the fourth world conference on women in beijing in 1995. as requested by the honourable members, it is important to focus on why and how obstacles to the achievement of equality between women and men still exist. i would also like to refer you to the annual report of the committee on equality between women and men, which was adopted on 14 february. before addressing the issues raised by the honourable members more directly, i would like to briefly outline some of the positive initiatives taken at eu level to promote equality between women and men. the promotion of equality between men and women has seen three milestones in the past decade, namely the adoption of the treaty of amsterdam, which created new competences in relation to the principle of equality between women and men. secondly, the establishment of a european employment strategy, which has made equal opportunities a key priority. finally, the integration of gender issues into different areas of action, including the social inclusion process and the structural funds through mechanisms such as the annual work programmes or the national action plans with targeted actions to promote gender equality. the european union's legislative framework on equal treatment has been steadily expanded over the years. the latest development was the adoption in december last year of a council directive which for the first time extends the principle of equal treatment beyond the field of employment and vocational training to goods and services accessible to the public. however, despite the progress made in gender equality, there is still a gap between equality in law and equality in practice and there are significant disparities between women and men in many areas, as also reflected in the presidency report. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the good news is that women's employment rates have increased by a greater proportion than men's over the last ten years, but the bad news is that the gap in employment remains very high at 17.2 percentage points and the pay gap between men and women remains virtually the same. this is a matter of concern not only for women but also for the european economy as a whole. if the european union is to achieve the ambitious goals of the lisbon strategy, it will have to reach the target of 60% employment by 2010. in line with the european employment strategy, member states have put in place mechanisms to achieve this objective in their national action plans. the objective set at the barcelona european council on the provision of childcare services is to facilitate women's entry into or return to the paid labour market. it is also part of the strategy to reconcile family and working life. considerable progress has already been made in this respect in many member states, although the traditional gender balance in childcare and paid work persists, despite efforts by some member states to implement policies to encourage fathers to take parental leave. the draft joint employment report this year, which will be submitted to the spring european council, also makes clear the need to strengthen concerted action to increase women's participation in the labour market, particularly with regard to the gender pay gap. in response to these concerns, ministers responsible for equality in the 25 member states committed themselves, in a declaration adopted on 4 february 2005, to developing strategies to increase the number of women in work and quality jobs for them, to guarantee and protect the rights of women in work and to remove structural, legal and psychological barriers to equality between women and men at work. the aim is also to promote policies that enable women and men to balance their work and private lives and their family responsibilities. the common indicators defined by the european union for the area entitled 'women and the economy', the sixth sensitive area identified in the beijing action programme, will make it possible to monitor the evolution of progress. the structural indicators defined in the framework of the european employment strategy will also be of great help in this process. violence against women: despite the many advances made in this area since the launch of the initial daphne programme in 1997, new measures are unfortunately still urgently needed to prevent and combat violence against women and children. we hope that the current daphne programme, which will run until the end of 2008, will remain an essential instrument for programming against violence. the projects carried out under this programme over the years have created many effective networks and developed good methodologies. a number of presidencies have tackled this problem, the most recent initiative being the adoption of indicators developed by the dutch presidency on sexual harassment in the workplace. in the above-mentioned declaration, the eu ministers responsible for equality between women and men agreed to develop preventive methods to combat gender-based violence and human trafficking and to monitor their implementation. they also decided to step up action to prevent and combat all forms of trafficking in women and girls through a coherent, multidisciplinary and coordinated strategy to combat trafficking in human beings. this strategy should be accompanied by measures to address all the factors that promote trafficking, by consolidating existing legislation to better protect the rights of women and girls, and by prosecuting and punishing perpetrators through both criminal and civil measures. as regards the wish to make 2006 the european year against violence against women, i do not deny that such an initiative could help to raise public awareness of this issue, but, according to the information i have, the commission intends to proclaim 2006 the european year of workers' mobility. it also announced that, in the context of promoting diversity and non-discrimination, 2007 would be the 'european year of equal opportunities' and it seems that 2010 should be proclaimed the 'european year of combating exclusion and poverty'. you may be interested to know that the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe has recommended to the committee of ministers that 2006 be proclaimed the 'european year against domestic violence' as part of a pan-european campaign carried out in cooperation with the european commission and the european parliament, as well as with national associations and ngos. women and poverty: in the ministerial declaration of 4 february, member states also agreed to step up the fight against social exclusion and to remove the obstacles to women's participation in the labour market, as a good job is one of the best ways out of poverty. although there are no gender-specific indicators on the feminization of poverty at eu level yet, some structural indicators, broken down by gender and developed in the context of the processes of inclusion and social cohesion, are presented each year at the spring european council. however, much remains to be done and in most national action plans in the member states, there is little consideration of gender issues outside the world of work. the issue of gender indicators could be addressed in the future. women and the environment: as regards the measures currently being taken to integrate the gender dimension into the development cooperation policy of the european union, i would like to remind you that last april the european parliament and the council adopted a regulation on the promotion of gender equality in the community's development cooperation policies, strategies and interventions. a financial framework of eur 9 million has been set for the period 2004 to 2006 for the implementation of this regulation. this follows the 1998 regulation which recognised that development actions have rarely properly addressed the differences between the situations, roles, opportunities and priorities of men and women and that correcting gender inequalities and strengthening the role of women are vital for social justice and the effectiveness of development efforts. i would also like to point out that the regulation was adopted in the context of the un millennium development goals, the un convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women, the beijing programme of action and the outcome document of the general assembly's special session entitled 'women in the year 2000: gender equality, development and peace for the 21st century'. at the 49th session of the un commission on the status of women, the presidency recognised, on behalf of the european union, that gender equality and the empowerment of women were essential to sustainable development and poverty eradication. girls: i have already touched on the issue of trafficking, but i would like to add that in a recent declaration, the eu ministers responsible for gender equality committed to mainstreaming a gender-sensitive approach at national level in immigration and asylum policies, regulations and practices, where appropriate, in order to promote and protect the rights of all women and girls, including by considering measures to take account of gender-based persecution and violence when deciding whether to grant asylum or refugee status. i would also like to point out that in april 2004 the council adopted a directive to grant residence permits to third-country nationals who are victims of trafficking in human beings. women's rights are human rights: the presidency, on behalf of the member states, reiterated its view to the committee on women's rights that full respect for all human rights and fundamental freedoms is essential to the emancipation of women and girls and the establishment of a genuine democracy. this view should continue to prevail in the negotiations in the council on the commission's forthcoming proposal for a fundamental rights agency. i should also add that the european union's new york declaration also addressed the need to combat harmful customary or traditional practices, including female genital mutilation, early or forced marriage and honour killings, which are considered obstacles to the full enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms by women and girls. women and armed conflict: the council took note of the european parliament's resolution calling for a 40% quota of women in posts related to reconciliation, peacekeeping and conflict prevention. there have indeed been discussions within the european union on the importance of the presence of women in peacekeeping forces and armies, and on the need to provide training for all to deal with the particular problems faced by civilian women in conflict zones. however, since there is no approved indicator or relevant statistical data on women and armed conflict, i am unfortunately not in a position to say whether or not the 40% quota has been met. in their statement of 4 february, eu ministers agreed to implement and encourage initiatives, policies and programmes in line with un security council resolution 1325 on women, peace and security, which does not set quotas as such but calls for increased participation by women. they also decided to act in accordance with the council of europe declaration, action plan and resolution on democratisation, conflict prevention and peace building. during the first week of the committee on women's rights' work, the european union outlined its commitment to promoting the role of women in conflict prevention and resolution, peacebuilding, democratic processes following conflict, as well as after disasters and during the reconstruction phases. the european union also stressed the importance of ensuring that women's needs in the context of post-disaster relief and reconstruction are well understood and programmed, and that women's access to disaster prevention information on an equal basis with men should also be ensured through formal and non-formal education, including gender-sensitive early warning systems. i would now like to conclude by thanking you for the opportunity to present on international women's day the european union's determination to achieve gender equality and its commitment to achieving the objectives set out in the beijing platform for action and the follow-up documents to the 55th session of the general assembly in 2000, which are still very much relevant today. i am confident that the european parliament and the commission will continue to work towards these same objectives and that by also involving civil society and ngos as much as possible, we can take further steps to promote equality. finally, i would not like to conclude without saying how pleased i am to see that today the commission is going to present its proposal for the european institute for gender equality, as it was invited to do by the european council in june 2004. such an institute will provide a much-needed tool and structure for finding a european-level response to issues such as the gender pay gap and increased access of women to the labour market, their participation in decision-making and work-life balance. campaign on the same subject and that, therefore, although there is no doubt about the importance of the initiative mentioned by parliament, the commission is reluctant to propose 2006 at european level, when 2004 was a year at world level. it is also important that gender issues are mainstreamed into health policies. this is done at european level through the public health programme, which has funded projects to develop strategies and establish good practices, for example in the areas of prevention of teenage pregnancy, family planning, prevention of sexually transmitted diseases. special attention is paid to hiv prevention in relation to mothers and children. efforts in the field of education should continue to prevent segregation from starting in school and spreading to the world of work. the european council and the commission have repeatedly highlighted the lower participation of girls in science and technology. it is therefore important that the education council set itself the target of increasing the number of graduates in mathematics, science and technology by 15% by 2010, while reducing the gender gap. the cornerstone of the european union's policy towards audiovisual media is directive 97/36 ec, television without frontiers. in its 2005 revision, the commission will present its proposal, which will take account of the rules relating to human dignity, in particular the anti-discrimination rules. the second important media tool is the recent draft recommendation on the protection of minors and human dignity and the right to reply with regard to competitiveness in the audiovisual sector and the european information services industry. it is important that media operators are given greater responsibility to ensure that discrimination is excluded from the content of their production. in our development assistance terms, we propose a strategy of gender equality as an end in itself and we recognise the central role of equality in development policies in poverty reduction, better governance and human rights. a modern society, based on creativity, on the ability to harness the human potential of all its members, cannot survive without harnessing the full potential of women. i think that's one of the main reasons for poverty in some parts of the world. the synergies between the platform and the millennium development goals shall be taken into account in the synthesis report on the progress made by the union and its member states towards the achievement of the millennium development goals. i would like to stress that women's rights are fundamental human rights, and the issue of equality between men and women in the european union goes beyond the respect of a fundamental right. this is a specific community policy, which is a priority, well-established in the treaties and supported by a very solid legal basis. as you know, the commission is preparing a proposal to extend the responsibilities of the vienna observatory for fundamental rights, and although it is premature to comment on the future work of the agency, it is clear that it will be concerned with the protection of fundamental rights for both men and women. ladies and gentlemen, in my previous speech i mentioned that the commission is today discussing the proposal to set up an institute for equal opportunities for women and men, the gender what i think is extremely important, which is a solid foundation, and give us more room for action with knowledge and without prejudice. ladies and gentlemen, thank you. states. these directives should have been transposed by july 2004, but transposition is still pending in some countries. i shall propose that the commission send a reasoned opinion to these countries next week and intend to pursue these infringement cases rapidly, with the aim of moving to the final stage of the procedure: referral to the court of justice in summer, if nothing happens. in addition, i have instructed my services to examine the implementing laws that have been adopted to ensure full conformity with the requirements of the directives. second, it is necessary to ensure a level playing field with respect to the detailed regulatory rules on issues such as tariff structures and third-party access rules. this has been pursued through the consensus-building approach of the florence and madrid forums which led to the regulation on cross-border trade in electricity that entered into force last year, and the equivalent regulation on gas, which we expect to be adopted very soon. these new laws will make a major contribution to the rapid convergence of detailed trading rules on electricity in each country. in this respect, the role of national energy regulators is central. the existence of such a regulator was a key requirement of the directives, and joint action by them will be vital in ensuring that, from the point of view of the customer, there is one single european electricity and gas network, not 25. it is for this reason that the commission established a european regulators’ group, which is beginning to provide important results in this direction. third, we need to examine whether the present legislative provisions are adequate to achieve our objectives of a truly competitive eu-wide market with high levels of consumer and environmental protection, as well as security of supply. in this respect the commission will make a detailed report to the european parliament and council at the end of this year on both the internal market and competition elements. this should in particular include a detailed examination of the adequacy of the already-existing measures. the report should form a basis for a detailed, wide-ranging debate that enables conclusions to be drawn in 2006. finally, it should be noted that the entry into force of the new constitution with a specific energy chapter would be of assistance in developing a coherent energy policy for the community, strengthening the existing legal basis for action.

ladies and gentlemen! the lisbon strategy is designed to ensure the prosperity, cohesion and development of european society. the achievement of these objectives requires the development of the means to achieve them. in parallel with the development of measures, it is important to keep the cost of living as low as possible. low prices for services and products are particularly important for the poorest groups of the population. the objectives of the lisbon strategy will be achieved, inter alia, by developing research to ensure access to modern technologies and by developing production to enable them to compete with non-eu countries. the efficient implementation of modern production methods, which allow the creation of modern and safe workplaces, should be a particularly important point. modern, low-cost and high-quality production enables competition on external markets, which in practice translates into the creation of new jobs in manufacturing and services. the implementation of the lisbon strategy involves analysing a number of areas of action by the european union and the member states. one of the key issues in the lisbon strategy is the proper orientation of research and implementation programmes. the existing system of scientific work management and research funding is widely used by the countries with the highest economic potential. for decades, flagship r & d centres have been established in europe, for example in finland and saxony. we have to create many new centres in five years to catch up with the leading countries in the world. we need to increase research spending to at least 3% of gdp, increase the scientific and research staff by at least 1 million people and put in place procedures to ensure that funds are spent efficiently. the current situation requires major organisational changes to ensure the coherence of the activities, e.g. the creation of a sufficient number of research centres, resulting from planned development of techniques, technology and production. these centres should concentrate on field research units. the newly organised research units should draw on the intellectual potential of countries that could not afford to build a modern research facility and thus conduct research on their own. the field units and research centres should, in addition to research, conduct teaching activities and recruit talented young people for doctoral studies, thus creating a pool of new research staff. such an action programme would fill the gap created by the drain of european personnel by non-eu countries. this scientific and technical base should largely benefit small and medium-sized enterprises whose growth is being driven by unemployment and which cannot afford to research and implement advanced and modern production methods. in the field of research, the creation of scientific staff and the coherence of these activities in the countries of the european union, there should be three programmes: the programme for the development of regions and the specialisation of production in the european countries, the programme for the development of the european system of scientific research and the training of scientific staff, and the programme for information, the introduction of new technologies and products for production. these programmes should minimise the adverse economic effects of the planned implementation of reach. the system of operation of the research and development base should be simple, clear and based on the principles of competitiveness, which should make it efficient and encourage private investment. the system must be coherent in order to gain social and political support... member of the commission. mr president, answering all these very important questions within two-and-a-half minutes is not very easy, but i will do my best. it is up to you to stop me when you think i have spoken long enough. i have been listening with great interest to all the various statements. i believe that we need an ambitious reform, a reform that actually brings the sugar regime into line with the 2003 cap reform, allowing farmers to take decisions that are market-driven and not based on political decisions. it must also be a reform that will enable the necessary restructuring of the sugar sector, to secure its long-term viability within the european union. as regards prices, let me be quite clear. maintaining prices at levels three times as high as world market prices is becoming increasingly difficult to justify and will certainly not lead to a sustainable european sugar sector. we also need a reform in order to live up to our international commitments. as for employment, the current regime does not guarantee the maintenance of jobs. over the last decade, 17 000 jobs have been lost as a result of continuous gains in productivity. if the current regime remains unchanged, it is estimated that there would be around 15 000 fewer jobs in 2012, a loss of more than 75%. the goal is therefore to achieve a competitive sugar sector in the community, so that the remaining jobs in the sector enjoy long-term sustainability. there were quite a few questions on impact assessment. the commission has carried out an impact analysis that gives a clear answer to the main questions relating to the reform proposal, including its regional effects. i am convinced that more studies will not provide us with facts that we do not already know. further analyses will just lead to a further delay in the decisions that we really have to take. on the point raised about ownership of quotas, under the current system the quotas for each member state are fixed by a council regulation. the member state then fixes the quantities each sugar producer is allowed to produce under the national quota, and the sugar producers themselves may then distribute sugar directly to the farmer on the basis of delivery rights. under the quota transfer system, as laid down in the commission communication of last july, quotas may be transferred between sugar-producing companies, against payment, across national borders. this would mean that companies have access to valuable quota rights, which can be transferred and then paid for. the normal way to achieve this would be to allocate quotas to companies. however, in the case of the transfer of a quota, the company concerned would not only have to use the money paid for the quota for its own restructuring, but also for compensating the sugar beet farmers for the devaluation of their delivery rights. as i mentioned in my introductory remarks, i can envisage a restructuring fund system. such a system could even leave the question of ownership of quotas untouched. the payments out of the fund could take the form of compensatory payments to farmers who suffered from the abandonment of sugar production in a given area. many members have criticised the transfer of quotas. i am willing to explore further the suggestion of a european restructuring fund, which could facilitate a quick exit from the sector by operators who might be interested in going out of business. this is an idea with tremendous legal, budgetary and political implications. however, provided it could be implemented in a safe and equitable way, a restructuring fund could be another tool that might be of great importance to our sugar restructuring objectives. it is clear that the reform will force farmers and producers to take important and sometimes difficult decisions about their future in the sector. we must offer them a clear outlook and, therefore, i consider predictability to be a key issue. i have taken note that this is a concern shared by parliament. i do not, therefore, intend to include the idea of a mid-term review in two or three years in the legislative proposals. instead, a long-term perspective should be offered. finally, let me summarise the main intentions of this reform. it is important to pursue the principles and objectives set out in the july communication. it is also important to have a long-term perspective, to bring prices and european production to a sustainable level and not to reopen the eba negotiations. then, with the help of the european parliament, we must reach a final political agreement before this summer.

mr president, i would like to draw your attention to the specific situation in which the treaty establishing a constitution for europe is now found. this treaty, signed in october 2004, is currently undergoing ratification and awaiting entry into force. the question then arises: what obligations do states have that have signed the treaty but have not yet ratified it? these obligations are laid down in international law, in particular the vienna convention on the law of treaties, which provides in article 18 that such a state has an obligation to refrain from actions which would impede or prevent the entry into force of that agreement or would compromise its object or purpose. this means that international law obliges governments to take all necessary steps to ensure the ratification of the european constitution. as a result, the state, the government, cannot in any way support or tolerate actions against the constitution, the pacta servanda sunt - treaties must be kept.

mr president, mr commissioner, in less than three weeks, the european union will have been enlarged for one year. for millions of citizens in central europe, it was the fulfillment of a dream of a common europe of fair rules and equal opportunities. in preparation for expansion, the new countries have opened their markets wide to the influx of western companies, goods, services and workers. they have done so very often in the atmosphere of heated internal debate and despite strong protests from many quarters, mainly workers, emphasising the need to protect domestic markets from unequal competition from the west, fearing the loss of their jobs. however, we understood that membership of the european union meant first and foremost participation in the common market, which guarantees freedom of economic activity throughout the community. at the same time, we were convinced that the european treaties set up fair rules for everyone, regardless of their country of origin. however, the last 11 months have provided numerous examples of discrimination against entrepreneurs and their employees from the new eu countries who intend to start their business in some of the 'old' eu countries. the most striking examples of discrimination occur in the netherlands, austria and italy. in these countries, the law allows for different treatment of companies and employees depending on whether they are from the "old 15" or the "new 10". this is particularly evident in the requirement to obtain work permits for posted workers before they start their activities. this procedure is always time-consuming, lasting up to 6 weeks in austria and is only applied to companies and workers from the new eu countries. the 'old 15' operators do not have to apply for a similar consent. in their case, a single page of information, together with a list of the staff seconded, lodged with the appropriate office shall suffice. they can therefore start the service without undue delay and any administrative control can be carried out during the execution of the order and without stopping the company's activities. this is therefore a clear example of discrimination sanctioned by national law, and the consequence of such regulations is to undermine the conditions of fair competition in the common eu market. in several other countries, however, despite the formal absence of discriminatory legislation, the behaviour of administrations and officials effectively prevents companies from the new member states from operating freely. i have in my hand complaints from businessmen who, despite meeting all the formal requirements, have been treated extremely negatively. control measures such as hand stamps, handcuffing, use of dogs, and even arrest, including abuse, were used against business owners and employees hired to carry out the orders. i regret to point out that germany and france are the countries where this type of behaviour is too common. i therefore ask the commissioner what action the commission intends to take to ensure that the treaty guarantees equality between companies and citizens. has the commission already analysed the member states' rules in order to guarantee fair conditions of competition for operators from the new eu countries? if so, what are the conclusions? if not, when will such an anti-discrimination review procedure be initiated? i would also like to stress the view, shared by many of my colleagues in this house, that without the commission's full commitment to combating discrimination against companies and workers mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the union has pursued a consistent policy of encouraging the development of enterprise and competitiveness in relation to economically backward countries which were late to join the european union, such as spain, portugal, greece and ireland. this was reflected in the facilitation of access to community markets and, consequently, in the surplus in the trade balance of the acp countries. this was one of the most important foundations for the rapid growth of employment, tax revenues, investment and, consequently, rapid economic growth. the facilitated access to community markets has enabled the least developed countries to significantly reduce the gap between them and the most developed countries. have the post-communist countries aspiring to the european union been given a similar opportunity? the answer is no. instead of solidarity and help, the union used its own strength, capital advantage, the subservience and corruption of the authorities, and the very fact of adoption delayed by forcing additional concessions. the most obvious manifestation of this policy was the negative balance of poland's trade balance with the european union, amounting to over eur 10 billion per year. it was not in poland, but in the union that jobs and profits were created. it was in poland, not in the union, that unemployment and poverty increased. what, then, was the opening of the polish market to eu companies and the subsequent accession of poland to the european union for polish companies? first, they allow for unequal competition with companies with technological and capital advantages. secondly, by allowing the takeover of polish companies, banks, financial institutions by the companies of the union, often not paying taxes in poland and not investing in poland, and worse, transferring profits abroad. thirdly, they were willing to bear the enormous costs and sacrifices of modernising companies to comply with the requirements, norms, standards of the union. fourthly, by agreeing to costly and burdensome administrative and bureaucratic procedures and regulations, by agreeing to tax arrangements that impair the
