the commission's vice-president mr president, first of all i should like to thank the rapporteur for his report and for his overall support for the commission's proposal. this proposal has its origins in two observations. firstly, reciprocity is a key principle in the field of visas. second, the mechanism provided for in regulation no 539/2001 to ensure that reciprocity is respected is inadequate, mainly because of its rigidity and automatic nature. as a result, the mechanism has never been used for more than three years, since the regulation actually entered into force, even though non-reciprocity situations persisted with regard to former member states and the number of non-reciprocity cases increased dramatically with the arrival of new member states. the commission has therefore proposed a more flexible and realistic mechanism, which is thus more credible and effective. each case of non-reciprocity will be notified. the commission will play an active role vis-à-vis the third country which introduced the visa requirement. it shall report to the council on the situation of non-reciprocity thus created and, if appropriate, propose the reintroduction of the visa requirement for nationals of the third country concerned. the amendments proposed by mr lax pursue three different objectives. the first objective is to extend the mechanism to cover a range of situations which are not only covered by the visa exemption but also by the conditions for issuing visas. this extension is contrary to the legal basis of the regulation. moreover, by attempting to cover a whole series of issues which are in reality of lesser importance, it would risk weakening the reciprocity mechanism which must remain focused on a key issue and felt as such by citizens: namely the maintenance of the visa requirement by third countries which are themselves exempted from this requirement by our member states. the hague programme confirms that this is a problem which must be tackled as a matter of priority. the second objective is to avoid situations of non-reciprocity lasting indefinitely and to include the possibility of responding with measures under the foreign policy. i share the general approach of this amendment and i must say to the rapporteur that the political orientation which emerged at the jha council on 24 february is along the same lines. however, i cannot accept that the commission's right of initiative be limited to a proposal for interim measures, nor, for reasons of legal basis, that the commission's right of initiative in this context be extended to proposals for measures in areas other than visa policy. the third objective is to involve the european parliament at all stages of the procedure. of course, the necessary transparency must be ensured, but the reciprocity mechanism must remain a flexible instrument which can be used quickly and which, and this is the essential point, must allow for an interim measure. the provisional reintroduction of the visa requirement for a third country is different from the transfer of that country to the list of visa-exempt countries annexed to regulation no 539/2001. such a transfer is an amendment to the regulation and as such is decided, of course, by the council after consulting the european parliament. finally, with a strengthened reciprocity mechanism, the commission will be equipped to respond to the solemn invitation addressed to it by the european council of 4 and 5 november 2004: to continue our efforts to ensure that citizens of all member states can, as soon as possible, travel without a visa for short stays in all countries whose nationals can travel to the union without a visa.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. mr president, the visa reciprocity mechanism that has operated so far in the european union's visa policy has meant very strict sanctions that could be applied to a third country after the notification of the country affected by the visa requirement. after the accession of 10 new countries, the european commission relaxed the rules of the regulation on 7 july last year, effectively eliminating the reciprocity mechanism in its draft. this has led to an absurd situation where 9 out of 10 new member states would have to accept third country nationals, such as the united states, without a visa, while our own citizens need a visa to travel to these countries. the report by mr lax, which i generally regard very highly, introduces some additional procedures and deadlines which can be applied by diplomatic means, but it does not impose on the council and the commission an obligation to apply more stringent sanctions. the fact that the european commission has the choice between imposing a visa requirement on third country nationals or introducing other measures which are much less effective is, in my view, too weak and does not sufficiently protect the citizens of the new countries. this approach clearly means that, when new countries join, it is difficult to speak of mutual solidarity between the countries of the union vis-à-vis third countries, and that, when new countries join, there is a double standard - a different mechanism for the union of fifteen, a different, less solidary one for the union of 25. this also exacerbates the differences in status between citizens of the new and the old union, with citizens of the new union subject to additional restrictions on travel outside the union. how can we talk about a new concept of european citizenship in this context if one part of the union's citizens enjoys completely different duties and rights than the other, inferior part? from the perspective of the new member states, the balance of costs and benefits of enlargement appears to be strongly skewed. on the obligations side, we have undertaken a costly operation to align with the union's visa policy, introducing visas for our eastern neighbours. on the positive side, we have little, we cannot yet issue schengen visas, we cannot count on the union's help in the matter of visa reciprocity. in addition, the member states of the union which require us to implement a common visa policy are themselves having problems with its implementation, as is evident in the case of germany. commissioner frattini, if the amended mechanism comes into force, i would like to state that we will enforce the commission's obligations. i also want to know specifically whether the commission can be expected to present an action plan with clearly defined deadlines for achieving the objectives of visa abolition for the usa and using the readiness of new countries to join the schengen area as a benchmark. this is in the vital interest of all citizens of the new member states.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin by thanking all those who have contributed to the quality of my report by providing valuable feedback. your involvement, which has been expressed in proposing amendments and in initiating numerous discussions and contacts, has been a testimony to me that the subject of my report is important to many of you. it's worth mentioning that this report is not just a collection of facts and statistical analysis, but also a use of my experience. for the last 15 years, i have run medium-sized businesses and learned firsthand what the conditions are for their continued growth and development. the internal market must become a single economic body, the driving force of the economy, and this will only happen when all member states correctly implement the directives relating to the internal market and all the others which are designed to improve it. it cannot be that some countries transpose and implement the directive and others do so laxly. the success of the internal market is closely linked to cooperation between countries and only joint efforts can bring about the results we all want. the european council, aware of this, set a deficit limit for all eu member states for the transposition of directives at 1.5%. the report examines the extent to which national transpositions of directives, and in particular of newly adopted ones, have performed surprisingly well. the lowest deficit at the beginning of november 2004 in transposing directives was 2.1%, compared with an eu-wide average of 5%. analysis of the same data, but one month later, at the end of november 2004, shows that the level of non-compliance in the new member states has fallen to 1.8% and the union average to 3.6%. the data provided clearly show how the transposition situation is improving. it took a month, a month of effort and commitment. and only then, when all countries transpose and implement the directives, can the remaining barriers to the movement of goods, people, services and capital be quickly removed, making the internal market a reality. i therefore propose, firstly, that the special infringement procedure introduced by the commission against new member states which have not transposed community legislation should become a universal norm and apply to all member states; secondly, that the 'scoreboard' of internal market performance be made an official document of the european council and be recognised as the main reference point for the state of transposition and that up-to-date data on the state of transposition of directives be made available to all member states on a regular basis; thirdly, that all member states which are lagging behind in transposition be marked by the success. in addition to the transposition and implementation of directives, it is worth noting the additional conditions that contribute to the development of the internal market and thus to the growth of the european economy. the key element is that new countries increase their investment in research and development, which is currently below the european average. they should also create better conditions for contacts between research institutions and businesses. as a citizen and former entrepreneur from the new member state, i also see the need for a more effective education and means a better quality of work. the existing union legislation should also be simplified, which will help to develop businesses, trade, services and the growth of the european economy. another element essential for the proper functioning of the internal market is the services directive. for new and old economies alike, the services directive is an opportunity to reduce unemployment, reduce regional ladies and gentlemen! the recent enlargement of the european union has created a new situation on the fruit and vegetable market. the union seemed fully prepared for this change, as the candidates were thoroughly 'scanned' in the annual reports. the european commission's analysis found that the new members will bring in as many as 19 fruit and vegetable species, which will increase the union's food self-sufficiency and consumer satisfaction. this knowledge, however, has not led to any change in the organization of the market, but we are faced with a curious situation: there is a special support mechanism for one variety of plums, and there is no such support for apples, the number one fruit, which accounts for 32% of the total fruit harvest. there is a support mechanism for nuts and bananas, but not for the whole range of soft fruit, which is inherently very fragile and therefore subject to price fluctuations. commissioner, the next season is running out and there are no responsible solutions. two policies are still in place: better for the old fifteen and worse for the new ten. instead of concrete solutions, the european commission seems to be acting in a false light. a special inspection was sent to poland. playing dead. this is a very dangerous game for the stability of the fruit and vegetable market, for the livelihoods of thousands of producers and their families, especially in the new member states, and finally for consumers exposed to price fluctuations and the need to import from third countries fruit of poor quality and posing a health risk. the point is simple: if the new member states guarantee the supply of soft fruit and high-quality apples, they must be supported as a matter of urgency, including by restricting imports, unless someone sees european solidarity differently and wants the common agricultural policy to cover other continents as well.
the enlargement of the european union to include ten new member states has made it necessary to modify the instruments of the common organisation of the market in fruit and vegetables in order to speed up the process of setting up producer groups and organisations and their effective functioning in order to prevent a disaster on this market. the degree of organisation of producers in the new countries is very low. in poland, it currently represents around 1,5% of the market. the new member states should receive increased aid for the maintenance and administration of the provisionally recognised producer groups. concrete financial support instruments are needed. the establishment of producer organisations should also be allowed for categories such as fruit for processing and vegetables for processing. it should also be noted that the market for soft fruit is characterised by a high price sensitivity due to the volatile level of their production and the increasing imports from third countries outside the union. as a result of uncontrolled imports, european farmers, including polish soft fruit producers, are now in a disastrous situation. action is needed to stabilise this market in the long term, including through the introduction of greater import controls to also prevent the influx of low-quality products. this check should be accompanied by the mandatory issue of a certificate of origin. the european commission should consider introducing import quotas for these sensitive products. what does the european commission propose? analysis and more specifically, indefinite actions, which means waiting and doing nothing.
the debate on simplifying the fruit and vegetable market today is giving rise to a more general reflection on the direction of changes in the common agricultural policy. as a member from the new member state, poland, i am surprised, as are many of my colleagues, that the philosophy of the eu approach to the economy, and agriculture in particular, is changing rapidly. when we were outside the union, we remember the union as a closed structure, as a closed market, which was very difficult for us to enter. and now that we are in the union, we hear the word liberalisation all the time. we're going to liberalize, open up our markets for fruit and vegetables, sugar, milk and everything else. we entered another union, and we are in another. as meps from poland, a country which produces half of the eu's soft fruit production, such as cherries, apricots and raspberries, we have asked the european commission several times in various forms to apply safeguard clauses to the soft fruit market and each time we have heard 'we, because liberalisation'. we must open our market to show solidarity with poor countries that want to export to our market. solidarity is a beautiful word, we value it especially in poland, but solidarity cannot be about transferring someone else's poverty to us. it cannot be that our farmers go bankrupt, that they themselves become poor, so that someone else in the union can sell their products instead. this cannot be the case, especially since there are serious concerns that liberalization will benefit speculators more than farmers in poor countries. i support the view that it is appropriate to apply safeguard clauses and restrict the import of fruit into the union market. i support mrs herranz's report in its entirety and appreciate the work she has done.
member of the commission. once again i should like to thank the committee for its own-initiative report on the simplification of the common market organisation for fruit and vegetables. i have listened carefully and i can assure you that the commission will analyse this final report very closely before presenting proposals for the fruit and vegetable sector. the presidency’s conclusions of november 2004 recognised that the path undertaken with the 1996 reform should be continued in the fresh fruit sector also. however, the commission was also asked to carry out an impact analysis on all aspects of processed fruit and citrus. that analysis will be available at the beginning of 2006. for the sake of coherence, the commission decided to present a global proposal covering both fresh and processed fruits. on crisis management, in the framework of the communication on risk and crisis management in agriculture, as well as the horizontal options identified in this context, the commission considers that specific needs should be looked at on a case-by-case basis in the context of the cmo reviews, even for the fruit and vegetable sector. accordingly, the commission will consider carefully the creation of a mutual stabilisation fund based on public and private co-financing. with regard to soft fruit, the council has also requested that the commission carry out the appropriate analysis of the new situation in the european market resulting from enlargement and, if necessary, bring forward proposals specifically to address these issues. the commission has already started the analysis of the soft fruit sector in the new member states. officials from the agriculture and trade directorates have just come back from a visit to poland. when this study is finished, we will analyse the results and, if necessary, appropriate measures will be taken in due course. as a member of the wto, we cannot adopt protectionist measures considered obstacles to imports. the most effective and efficient way to respond to market signals is to focus on the quality of our products and improve the competitiveness of our sector. we could do that using two different tools. as i have already said, one involves strengthening producers’ organisations, so that we prevent producers from competing against one another; and the second, the possibility of strengthening our promotional initiatives, which could be helpful. some of you raised the issue of the import of fruit and vegetables from third countries, in particular red fruits. third country imports have to meet the standards that we apply in the community. member states must check products entering into the community and should notify the interception of non-compliant products to the commission through our rapid alert system. based on the information that we have, provided by that system, only three interceptions of fresh and frozen fruit, which did not meet our standards, took place in the period from january 2002 to april 2005. given the large quantity that is imported, it is my opinion that this is a very small amount. as regards the introduction of special labelling of origin, i can assure you that i will be positive in my approach to that. i can only stress the great importance of this specific sector to the member states, both from an economic and a job-creation point of view.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on wednesday at 11.30 a.m.
the next item is the report by mr janusz wojciechowski (a6-0096-2005) on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development on the draft council regulation amending regulation (ec) no 1868/94 establishing a quota system for the production of potato starch (com (2004) 772 - c6-0014/2005 - 2004/0269 (cns)).
member of the commission. mr president, i shall start by thanking mr wojciechowski and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for all the work they have carried out on this report. i would like to place this proposal in its context. on 26 june 2003, the council adopted a fundamental reform of the common agricultural policy which significantly changes the way that the european union supports the agricultural sector. as far as potato starch is concerned, 40% of the aid paid to the producer has been decoupled and included in the single farm payment scheme. after enlargement, six of the ten new member states have been involved in the potato starch quota system for the first time in 2004-2005 marketing year. since the potato starch production quotas were introduced in 1995, we have been trying to define a strategy to secure, enhance and promote the development of this very important sector. i return to the proposal discussed today. it is of vital importance to preserve the stability of this fragile sector, while at the same time taking into account the fundamental changes due to the reform of the cap and enlargement. firstly, to roll over the quotas for two years instead of the three years foreseen in regulation (ec) no 1868/94. this time-frame should allow us to analyse the initial effects of the cap reform and enlargement on the potato starch sector and enable us to act quickly should the need arise. secondly, to roll over the existing quotas which have provided a stable market in the eight old member states taking part in this regime. i am well aware of the fears in certain new member states that their quotas negotiated in their accession treaties and based on a historical reference period might be too small. as usual, the development of the potato starch sector in all member states will be closely monitored in the years to come. the commission appreciates the contribution of the agriculture committee to the development of this area. several of the proposed amendments, however, go beyond the scope of the commission’s proposal, especially as far as the time-frame for the proposal is concerned. because a prolongation of four years would not allow us to react quickly to possible imbalances in the european starch market, the commission cannot accept this amendment in the context of the proposal at hand. the amendment concerning the transfer of quotas to new member states certainly raises issues of great importance to the countries concerned. however, experience has shown that the starch potato yield fluctuates a lot, depending on climatic conditions. allowing for the possibility of transnational balancing-out, with priority given to the new member states, might incite starch producers in these member states to increase the areas under contract, hoping for a transfer of unused quotas from other member states, which could lead to a significant overshoot of their quotas in years when the climatic conditions in the european union are favourable for potato growing, thus aggravating their situation. in conclusion, the commission cannot accept the amendments proposed in the report.
the house of lords! the committee on agriculture has had a problem with this report - firstly, how long and secondly, how much? how long is the current quota system to be extended for, and secondly, whether to make adjustments in the amounts? on the first point, the committee on agriculture considered that the wine quota system should be extended not for two years, as proposed by the commission, but for four successive marketing years. the argument prevailed that this period should be sufficiently long to allow potato and starch producers to establish their production plans in a timely manner. the two-year period proposed in the draft is insufficient for this and therefore the committee on agriculture has adopted an amendment and proposed a longer period of four years. the second issue, whether to adjust the amounts, was an emotional one. much of the discussion focused on the unfair treatment of the new member states, which were allocated amounts inadequate to their production potential in the accession negotiations. of the total quota of 1 947 000 tonnes allocated to the 25 countries of the union, 89% is allocated to the 15 countries and only 11% to the 10 countries. commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is easy to see from the statistics that back in 1999 the ten had more potatoes than the fifteen, 1 600 000 hectares, whereas the fifteen had about 1 400 000 hectares. in the following years, this has changed somewhat, as potato production in the g10 countries has declined sharply, but it is still very high. the example of poland, which is the largest potato producer in the european union and, despite the closure of a large part of the plantations, is still the largest potato producer, with production quantities several times lower than those of germany, the netherlands or france, was given in the discussion. as a result of the undercutting, poland, the potato powerhouse, produces less starch than it needs to meet its domestic demand and has to import significant amounts of starch. other new countries have similar problems, most notably lithuania. on the other hand, it was pointed out that the countries of the 15 with high production quotas of starch have not used up their quotas in full for years, e.g. in the last 6 years only in one year 2001 we had 100% utilization of quotas, and in the other years the non-use was between 3% and 17%. it was pointed out that it was unfair that some countries were not using the quotas while others were suffocating because they were not getting enough. however, the committee on agriculture considered that there could be no question of increasing the global quota or of changing the quota allocated to individual countries, mainly because of the fear of a market collapse in the event of higher production. the committee on agriculture, on the other hand, has come up with a different idea, the result of a broad compromise, to propose what is known as balancing - the possibility of carrying over amounts when they are not fully used. in view of the difficult situation of the new member states, the committee on agriculture proposed that if the allocated amounts were not used - as has often happened recently - the unused part should be transferred to the new member states in the first instance. that is, madam president, a very good solution - we are not increasing the overall production quota, we are not endangering the market, we are not undermining the delicate structure of the system, but we are creating the possibility of equalising the unfair distribution of quotas, at least when some countries do not use their quotas. i would like to thank very warmly the members of the committee on agriculture from all the political groups for having accepted this compromise proposal without a single vote of opposition and i recommend this compromise to the house and to the commission, commissioner, with the deep conviction that the balancing proposal should be included in the new draft regulation. i would like to stress once again that this is a very wise and necessary compromise, which is an expression of the solidarity of the old and new member states, a solidarity which we so badly need.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, one of the small parts of the reform of the common agricultural policy is the reform of the starch market. the report and the explanatory statement, although it concerns a very narrow section of the common agricultural policy, is the best example of the differences and irregularities between the individual countries, which the mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament is not a party to the treaty of rome. in speaking about the quota system for potato starch production, i would like to draw attention to three points which i consider important. firstly, it is very common in agricultural debates to get the impression that the commission representatives do not have, or do not want to have, full knowledge of the productive potential of the new countries. in the case under discussion, namely potato starch production, the production potential of the new member states amounts to 30% of the production of the whole union, whereas the production quotas for starch represent only about 10% of the production quotas of the whole european union. there is therefore no doubt that the distribution of these amounts between the old and the new member states is grossly unfair. secondly, it is very common in discussions to hear that everything that has been achieved in the accession negotiations cannot be changed, because any change that is beneficial for one country would trigger the desire of the other countries to improve their situation - an approach that cannot be accepted. thirdly, the commission's reaction to the speeches and motions of the members of parliament is extremely slow and often takes weeks, and months, to act in practice. this is also unacceptable. i hope, therefore, that despite these reservations, at least on the production quotas for starch the commission, the council and parliament will be able to reach a compromise. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'common carrier' to cover all transport services. this solution does not guarantee the new member states certainty about increasing their starch production quotas, but it does at least provide an opportunity to do so, especially since the amount of starch produced in the european union has been on average 7% below the current production limits per year for the last six years. so it is likely that the future will be similar. under the new regulation, unused amounts will be able to be transferred to the new member states. this will create an opportunity for farmers growing starch potatoes in these countries, in particular in poland, to improve the income situation of their holdings and allow the starch industry to make better use of production capacity.
member of the commission. thank you for your contributions to this important debate. one of the points raised by several members concerned the question as to why the new member states did not get a higher quota from the very beginning. the potato starch quotas for the new member states were negotiated in copenhagen in 2002 and agreed by the candidate countries and the eu-25. they were calculated in exactly the same way as quotas for other member states, taking an average of the production during a three-year reference period. as regards the example of poland that was mentioned, let me offer a few figures. average production in poland from 1999 until 2001 was 107 317 tonnes; nevertheless, a quota of 144 985 tonnes was granted to poland. therefore, to talk of unjust quota does not seem entirely justified. i fully recognise the importance of poland as a producer of potatoes, but let me remind you that starch quotas are based on historical production and not on the potential of the different member states. the other issues concern the extension of the time frame to four years and the possibility of quota transfer to the new member states. in my opening statement i made it clear that i cannot accept the amendments proposed in the report.

your honour, today in the european parliament we commemorate the 60th anniversary of the end of the second world war, the most terrible war in history, which brought the death of millions of people, the extermination of the jews, which plunged europe into the abyss of barbarism, economic ruin and moral decay. we bow to that time and honor the memory of the victims of that war. your honour, there are moments in the memory of societies that are special, really important, that allow us to be together in the work of building a political community. the european nations have their own memories of the 20th century. this is the result of the historical experience of the various political events in our countries and our societies. but there is a memory that unites us, the memory of the victims of war, the memory of the struggle for freedom and democracy, the memory that forms our common european identity. today we remember the victims of nazi terror in the countries occupied by the third reich. we commemorate the victims of the shoah, the genocide of the european jews during the second world war, a crime of a unique character in the history of all mankind. we celebrate the victory of the allied powers over the third reich, and especially the role played by the united states of america in the liberation of europe. we remember all the soldiers who died to free the world from nazism, the 14 million soldiers of the red army. we honour the memory of the victims of all sides in the second world war, we commemorate the wartime victims of stalin, whose symbol was the massacre of some 22 000 polish citizens and prisoners of war in katyn and other camps and prisons in the soviet union in the spring of 1940. we pay tribute to the fighters for freedom, democracy and human rights, and we remember in particular the heroic resistance movement fighting in individual countries against fascism and occupation. a resistance movement whose ideals and sacrifice in an unequal struggle are today our true heritage, a cause of common pride and an example for the younger generations of europeans. today i would like to commemorate the resistance movement in the warsaw ghetto, the insurgents of the jewish combat organization, who took up the fight on april 19, 1943, on the territory of the ghetto for the jewish population created in warsaw by the occupying authorities. a fight which, in the midst of war, in the midst of nazi-ruled europe, had no chance militarily, a fight which, however, had a deeper meaning, whose heroism is for us today the highest testimony of the human spirit and one of the moral foundations of the europe we are building. as the jewish fighting organization put it, "the fight is for your freedom and ours, for your and our human, social, national honor and dignity". your honour, we remember that not all european nations saw the end of the war as a true liberation, independence and democracy. for central and eastern europe and the baltic states, the end union. for estonia, latvia and lithuania, also the loss of independence and incorporation into the soviet union. socialists, social democrats, the democratic left, in the 20th century, were against all forms of dictatorship, against all non-democratic regimes. we are a political movement that has always stood for democracy and human rights. in the baltic states, in central and eastern europe, and in those countries of southern europe which were ruled by dictatorships after world war ii: portugal, spain and greece. your honour, i say this in the european parliament, in strasbourg, in a territory marked by war and the collapse of europe. our ancestors met on this land, facing each other as soldiers. we are here today as citizens, as members of parliament representing a united europe. the answer to the wars since the 1950s has been european integration, the creation of the european community. the creation of the european institutions has been and is the process of overcoming the conflicts between the peoples of europe. the european union today is the product of three great democratic processes: the defeat of fascism in war, the fall of dictatorships in southern europe in the second half of the 1970s and the triumph of democracy in central and eastern europe and the baltic states. our continent is building an international order based on peace and cooperation. a community is being established based on the principles of respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights, including the rights of persons belonging to minorities. the european union, a union of 25 countries, today embraces a society with a diverse history. the ratification of the constitution for europe will mean the creation of a united europe, mr. speaker, the house! the future of europe sixty years after the end of the second world war depends to a large extent on the fulfilment of two basic conditions: first, the recognition by all of the historical memory of the events of the second world war, and second, on the basis of this memory, the construction of a common vision of european integration. historical memory can differ depending on whether the end of the war was or was not a true liberation. from my country's perspective, it's a reminder of a few key dates that sealed the tragic history of world war ii. september 1, 1939 - hitler's invasion of poland and the beginning of a nightmarish period of occupation, repression, camps, occupation activities leading to the destruction of the nation and society, but also a period of heroic acts of the state and underground society. september 17, 1939, a date unfortunately less known in western europe, but painful and significant for us - the soviet invasion of poland under the pact ribbentrop-molotov, which means: hitler-stalin and the further dismemberment of poland. 1943 - the disclosure of the katyn crime committed in 1940 on stalin's orders by murdering several thousand polish officers and officials, only because they were in the service of the polish state. 1943 and 1944 - two more heroic uprisings: the uprising in the warsaw ghetto ended with its bloody stream, or rather extermination, and the warsaw uprising, whose stream was passively watched from the right bank of the vistula by soviet troops. 1945 - member of the commission. mr president, this has been a very useful, rather balanced and proportionate debate, but i well understand the huge anxieties and sensitivities that are excited by this issue of textiles. let me say that, of all the contributions made since the opening remarks, if i had to identify one contribution with which i was most in sympathy and which most corresponded to my own views and approach, it would be that of mr calabuig rull, because stressing that we need to see china as an opportunity as well as a potential threat and that the containers that are heading towards europe with all these textiles and other goods and produce need then to be sent back to china filled with european goods and produce hits exactly the right note. when i talk about goods and produce i also mean a huge potential and expanding market for european services. i agree that we need to help the textiles industry in europe to restructure and adapt, and we are giving that assistance. i agree that, if china is to have its own growth accepted by the international economic community, then it needs to reciprocate by opening its own markets to others’ produce and to comply with international agreements. however, i also agree that, if, in the circumstances of this very sudden and very dramatic surge in chinese exports, we have to take action on our side in order to manage this transition and to smooth these changes, then that action is open to us to take. it may be limited in terms of its content and its duration. none of us should exaggerate – especially for those who are directly concerned with these changes – what is at our disposal to do in order to counter this. at the very least, we can limit the growth of chinese exports on a temporary basis. it is not open to us, under the wto rules, to do more than that. however, where the facts justify our doing that, i, certainly, and my colleagues in the commission will not shrink from doing so. it is easy in a debate like this to talk in generalisations. what we cannot do is act in generalisations. we have to act on a case-by-case basis and on the basis of the facts. why? because we must act in a way that is legally defensible. the worst course of action for us in the commission would be to act in a way that we could not subsequently defend, only to find ourselves challenged in the wto and forced to reverse the actions we have taken. that would be a tremendous disappointment and setback for those who are most directly affected, and we must be careful. therefore, we must enforce the rules, but we cannot invent the rules. that is what we must bear in mind throughout this. also, there is a mixed picture developing in terms both of the impact of import levels on particular commodities and categories of textiles and of the impact on production levels and employment within different parts of the european textiles industry. not just in the united states, but in some cases also in europe, import levels are falling. in other cases, chinese imports and their growth are displacing the imports from third countries. so it is a mixed picture. in terms of the impact of these trade flows on european production and employment, it is true that, in some cases, the impact appears to be dramatic, based on the facts that i was reviewing with my services only yesterday, facts, for example, from greece, portugal and italy. there are some very disturbing developments. i have to take note of those and i have to base my future actions on those facts. in the case of some of our other member states, i have yet to receive the relevant data and the relevant information. even certain member states at the forefront of the demands for me to adopt emergency and urgent procedure have not sent me the facts on which i could base such urgent action. however, i am sure it will be forthcoming. mr caspary, mrs mann and mr martinez raised interesting questions and ideas, and i will write to them in response in due course. finally, the statement made yesterday by the chinese premier wen jiabao, in which he seems to have decided to give instructions to relevant government departments in china to prepare effective action to curb chinese export growth, is welcome to me. we need, however, to look at the reality of these actions, when they are agreed, and consider the impact they will have. in the light of those, the commission will consider what future action it will take from here on.

ladies and gentlemen! the draft directive under discussion imposes a legal obligation on lawyers practising the profession to identify, record and disclose to the financial services of the state confidential information provided by a client in the course of providing legal aid. as a practicing lawyer, i can say with full conviction that this solution significantly affects the independence of the legal profession and violates the observance of professional secrecy, which is one of the fundamental principles of the profession. a lawyer who is required to work for a third party from the very beginning of his client's dealings becomes a witness for the prosecution, or his client's worst enemy. in conclusion, the scope of the proposed directive constitutes an excessive interference with the exercise of the legal profession. in order to ensure the proper functioning of the judiciary and the existence of genuine and not a sham defence, it is necessary to exclude acts of professional secrecy from the scope of activities aimed at combating money laundering.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the subject of our discussions is a proposal for a council directive amending articles 7, 8, 9, 10 of directive 92/12 eec. i would remind you that the directive contains general provisions on the marketing and storage of products subject to excise duty, in particular alcohol and tobacco products, but also liquid fuels. i would also point out that article 27 of the 1992 directive required the commission to submit a report to the council on the operation and application of articles 7, 8, 9 and 10 for the period up to 1997. for various reasons explained by the commission, this report on the application of those articles is only being discussed today, after a delay of several years. i would point out that article 7 concerns the marketing of excise goods by undertakings for commercial purposes, article 8 concerns the marketing of excise goods by individuals for personal purposes, article 9 defines the moment when the tax liability arises and sets out the indicative limits to be used to determine whether the excise goods transported are of a commercial nature or are intended for individual use. finally, article 10 lays down the manner and place of the tax liability, the obligations of tax intermediaries and the conditions of distance sales, the so-called distance sales conditions. the determination and application of these articles in practice has raised a number of doubts, both among individuals, travellers and tourists, and among undertakings professionally engaged in the trade and circulation of excise goods. the commission has therefore decided to propose some amendments to the wording of the four articles mentioned above, with a view to two main principles. first, the commission wanted to apply consistently the principle of the single market, namely that excise duty is paid in the country of destination for trade. however, for the sale by persons buying excise goods for their own use, excise duty was to be levied in the country of origin of the goods. the commission therefore proposes to amend article 7 to define what constitutes trade and, according to the commission's definition, any trade which is not for personal use is trade. further amendments to article 7 concern the simplification of the language and the use of more precise wording. finally, the commission also proposes in article 7 to clarify who is liable to pay the tax. the commission is introducing a very important amendment to article 7, namely that the purchase of goods by private individuals need not necessarily take the form of the transport of those goods by the persons concerned and that it should also be possible for private individuals to order excise goods at a distance with delivery to their place of residence. this also applies to so-called gifts. it is therefore the introduction of the principle that trade for personal use is possible not only when the traveller carries goods with him but also when someone carries goods on his behalf and at his expense. in article 9, the commission proposes an important change, namely the abolition of quantitative limits which have hitherto been used against their intended purpose. finally, in article 10, the commission again proposes to make certain changes to simplify the procedure. the rapporteur is of the opinion that all changes to tax law in the european union should meet four criteria; they should follow the logic of the single market, i.e. they should prevent discrimination. second, they should be simple and clear so that they can be easily applied. thirdly, they should not lead to drastic violations of the level of budget revenues in individual countries. fourthly, they should also meet certain health policy standards, if such policies are in place in the individual countries. the rapporteur considers that the commission's proposals are in line with these criteria and i therefore support these amendments in general, while the amendments we propose concern mainly the linguistic corrections and the better wording of the various provisions, the use of more precise terms, and we also propose that the administrative authorities of the individual member states should be required to prove whether goods are intended for commercial use when implementing these provisions. in the past, this has been too often the responsibility of travellers and we believe that this is incompatible with the rules of the common market. in general, the amendments which are applied are amendments which merely put the text in order and, in a sense, clarify it further, whereas all the commission proposals are supported.

ladies and gentlemen! despite the strong rejection of the draft constitutional treaty in france and the netherlands - a clear indication of mistrust of national and european political elites - we are surprised to see some attempts to revive the document. there is talk of continuing the ratification process, renegotiating the draft treaty, or even seeking legal solutions to annul the results of the referendums. such actions are undemocratic and arrogant, and they are a form of totalitarianism. the political elites should realize that most of the nations of europe oppose the organization of a bureaucratic "super state" run from brussels, monopolizing social, economic and monetary policy. they want democratic participation in decision-making and european integration based on the free cooperation of free states. heads of state and government who do not respect the sovereign will of the people can be seen as dictators by their own people and treated as such.

mr. chairman, please! after the french and dutch referendums, we were inundated with a flood of analysis, interpretation and speculation. one of the most frequent is that the negative results are a protest by the citizens of these countries against the recent enlargement of the european union. they're sort of a punishment for what happened a year ago. the conclusion to be drawn from this is that the only way to stop further enlargement is to wait for the european union boa constrictor to swallow and digest the rabbit, which is the new member states. there are already voices, including in this chamber, questioning the decision to join bulgaria and romania on 1 january 2007. the decision to open negotiations with turkey in october is openly questioned, and ukraine's european aspirations are put on hold. of course, no one can be prevented from expressing such opinions, but it would be a serious mistake to follow them up with restrictive policy decisions, for at least three reasons. firstly, we must not break the commitments we have made to ourselves and to the people of the countries applying for membership of the european union. the rules, i remind you, are to be followed not when they are convenient - when they are unnecessary - but when they are difficult to follow. second, each successive extension has always been an economic success. thirdly, the european union is not to be an elitist, closed club, but on the contrary an open space for democracy, respect for human rights, respect for minorities and peaceful means of resolving conflicts. for me, that last consideration is particularly important. this is not only the essence of the european community, but its mission. without this mission, not only will the constitutional treaty be dead, but the union itself.

in writing. the moraes report on minority protection contains, in its final version, provisions aimed at a very risky treatment of the rights of sexual minorities. the risk is that they are understood too broadly, because of the overly broad concepts used in the report. the wording of article 24 calling on the commission to remove obstacles to freedom of travel within the eu by means of marriage or legal same-sex unions may become the basis for the recognition of selected legal consequences of homosexual unions, which are legally recognised only by some eu countries. this would lead to unjustified interference in the family law system of some eu countries, which is unacceptable given the fact that this area of law is outside the area of integration. article 22 may be used to restrict the religious rights of educational institutions by imposing an obligation on them to employ homosexuals and to include such content in sex education curricula. this may be contrary to the ethos of these institutions, as well as their beliefs and mission (an example of a directive that omits this aspect is the equal treatment in employment and occupation directive (2000/87/ec)). despite the insistence, parliament did not introduce a provision emphasizing "the right of parents to raise their children in accordance with their own religious convictions". this formulation of parental rights is a widely accepted standard of international law. in view of the above decisions of parliament, i have decided to vote against the report and resolution.

whether something is efficient or not is decided by those who run companies according to the sound principles of the free market. then, in paragraph 6, we read: "women should be encouraged to work in industry". ladies and gentlemen, this is a deep-seated feminist contamination. women don't have to be encouraged to work in industry, they'll work wherever they want. i don't see any reason for women to work with jackhammers. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be able to take account of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a decision on the compatibility of the aid with the internal market. ladies and gentlemen, this is not the way to be competitive and successful. 130 years ago, the prime minister of england, then the world's fastest-growing nation, said: "the job of economists is to make sure that government does not harm the economy". i do not expect the european commission to follow these guidelines, but i would urge it to at least take them into account.

mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to stop. the considerations in mrs vlasto's report are mature and balanced. they represent a stage in the debate on european industrial policy. europe is in crisis over this policy, and citizens are expressing their irrational fears and frustrations, for example, in the referendums in france and the netherlands. the fact is that relocation, while seemingly economically justified, is undoubtedly socially harmful. however, when it comes to delocalisation, it is important to emphasise that it is a heterogeneous concept, with regard to both beneficial - due to the positive synergy - intra-eu delocalisation and harmful external delocalisation. a homogeneous market for goods and services with a high degree of global competitiveness and innovation should be created. there are two groups of mechanisms for increasing competitiveness: the simple ones limiting the achievements of the so-called european social model, and the complex ones based on intellectual and social capital, which are the basis for organisational, technological, technical and market innovation. europe, like japan and europe in the late 1960s, should resort to relocation, i.e. the return of modern manufacturing and capital to the european common market. this is necessary to protect intellectual property and restore european leadership in know-how, create jobs and increase the competitiveness of european capital. all of this is possible, but first europe must break out of stagnation and its gdp should grow at least several times. the tools that would undoubtedly help trigger the relocation process could include - contrary to the frustrations and fears of the proverbial polish plumber and bricklayer - full liberalisation of commercial services, as the polish socialists argue, the creation of industrial clusters around the innovation centre, the introduction of european rules for all public procurement, which would require the preparation of an appropriate eu directive.

substantial contribution from the commission. according to the european security strategy, our security is now subject to many new threats, many new challenges. the most significant are the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, but also the spread of international terrorism. the fact that the terrorism that we were used to in the 1970s and 1960s in europe has been replaced by a new terrorism that is much more far-reaching, much more lethal, much more dangerous. this means that without advanced technological tools, it is difficult to ensure the safety of our citizens today. it is also difficult to give credibility to our security and defence policy. the european union currently spends four times less on defence investment than the united states. research and development costs are five times less. and that's why our countries are not able to close the technological gap between the defense and security capabilities of the united states and us here in europe. in response to this need for more effective safety research, the commission has therefore proposed a european safety research programme under the seventh framework programme, which is due to start in two years' time. this programme will focus on research projects that enhance our technological capabilities, based on a coherent, flexible and coordinated approach. there is currently a lack of a coherent approach to safety research at the highest level of the union, resulting in a high level of fragmentation and lack of cooperation between member states. this also results in low cost-effectiveness of these studies. therefore, the creation of common frameworks and structures at european level by establishing a european security research programme will allow for interoperability on the one hand and cost optimisation on the other. this programme envisages the exploitation of the synergy between the military research sector and the civil research area. it can therefore be expected that the programme will promote the integration of these two sectors. moreover, the adoption by the european parliament of this programme, whose annual budget is proposed at the level of one billion euros in addition to the funds already allocated to research in this field by the individual member states, should reduce the differences between our european countries and the united states. thus, strengthening the research base and the innovation of solutions will stimulate increased competitiveness in europe. we can count on this programme to be an opportunity for our european industry, but member states of the european union. the report shall identify priority areas of interest. i'll just tell you a few. first, the so-called c4isr kit, which is the command, communications, guidance, intelligence, reconnaissance and reconnaissance systems. but also research in biotechnology, space technology and information systems. the report also encourages the commission to support research in mr. chairman, please! the legal status of computer programs has long been settled. the software is copyrighted. the european patent convention excludes the patenting of computer programs. both legal theorists and computer scientists are opposed to changing this situation. it is only the practice of the european patent office which is to be sanctioned by a council directive, and that is bad and dangerous. i therefore call on behalf of professor buzek and myself for support for all 21 amendments to the package which restore the directive to its original meaning or for the directive to be rejected in its entirety. as the german parliament stated in its resolution of 17 february this year, patent inflation risks undermining the public's acceptance of the patent system as an effective tool for innovation and progress. it is therefore the responsibility of the european parliament to apply the safety brake in such a situation. there is no need to add further patent protection to computer programs. the main argument for the introduction of patent law was the need to protect investments. material innovation requires long-term experimentation and then capital investment before it can be profitable. however, investment in information goods is usually low, if at all. there is therefore no need for additional legal protection for them. it's also not true that software patenting, as the european patent office understands it, is an opportunity. patents also carry dangers and should therefore be used with caution. patent myths and half-truths abound. i'll name a few. granting patents is always good for the economy -- that's a myth. officials often measure economic innovation by the number of patents. however, patents can harm investment by restricting competition. a large number of the leading computer companies never applied for patents. hardly anyone in the computer science field is interested in patent descriptions. and no one has been able to prove a direct link between patent expansion and economic growth. the second myth is that software patents can help small and medium-sized enterprises because they give them exclusive rights to their innovative ideas. patents, however, not only protect, but also block. it's very difficult for smaller companies to get protection because the cost of enforcing a patent is very high, up to 100 times the cost of getting a patent. in addition, there is the need to make a difficult discovery of whether someone else has already reserved something. in the case of computer science, with the particular ease of introducing a slight variation, patenting them is creating a kind of minefield.

in writing. the three main aspects of energy security that were not adequately addressed in the draft directive of the european parliament and of the council are:• the aspect of increased use of renewable energy sources,• the sustainable use of different types of primary fuel,• the differentiation of supplies from different production centres (oil and gas fields) within one type of primary fuel. i think it is very harmful to maintain a european policy in this area which, in the name of security, leads to poland's total dependence on a single source of supply, namely russian oil and gas. the advanced concept of the second yamal pipeline strand should be continued. all other projects (the baltic sea pipeline project and the so-called 'amber pipeline') should be immediately abandoned as a direct threat to the newly reborn ukrainian democracy. the energy security of the uk, germany and italy should not be achieved at the expense of poland's dependence on russian oil and gas and the threat to ukraine's economic stability.
in writing. "the draft directive of the european parliament and of the council concerning measures to safeguard security of electricity supply and infrastructure investment regulates many areas of common european energy market. i indicate three major aspects of the energy security which are not adequately underlined: · enhanced use of renewable energy sources· balanced use of various types of primary fuels· diversification of supplies from various production centres (oil and gas fields) within one type of the primary fuel. i consider it totally unacceptable to maintain the european policy in this respect leading, in the name of security, to complete dependency of poland on one source of supply, namely russian gas and oil. the well advanced in concept project of the second route of the jamal gas pipeline should be continued immediately. all the other projects (baltic sea bottom pipeline or so called "amber pipeline") should be abandoned as striking directly in newly emerging ukrainian democracy. energy security of great britain, germany and italy should not be achieved at the cost if polish dependency and a threat to ukrainian economic stability."
the rapporteur. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: let me make a few comments on the report. i'll try to speak as a reporter, not as a representative of my political party. cross-border cooperation is one of the most visible and effective ways of building personal bonds and good relations between local, regional and national communities. crossborder cooperation already has a rich tradition and has achieved significant successes over many years. different forms of organization have also developed. the european union, aware of the many benefits of this form of international cooperation, supports it both within the union, at its borders and in regions far from each other, and at its external borders, using various types of financial instruments. the current programming period is the time of many activities of a cross-border, transnational and interregional nature. i am using the terminology of the interreg iiia, iiib and iiic programmes here. the regulation in question is a new legislative proposal which can contribute both to strengthening the many forms of crossborder, transnational and interregional cooperation and to facilitating the conduct of joint ventures and to improving the efficiency of the use of funds allocated to this purpose. the new regulation gives public authorities at all levels the possibility of setting up a new instrument in one of the selected countries, which will have legal personality in the country of establishment and will then be notified to all member states, the european commission and the committee of the regions - as i propose in my report. the bodies which make up the european cooperation grouping, as the original text says, crossborder and as i propose in my report, territorial, will be able to delegate to it selected public services and to entrust it with some of its tasks as provided for by the rules. the creation of this instrument is perhaps one of the first proposals in the history of the european union to create a truly european entity and at the same time to strengthen the implementation of the principle of subsidiarity in practice. i think that the european parliament should support this idea and thus give a very clear and measurable signal of its support for these actions at local, regional and national level, but also at interlocal, interregional and inter-state level, which are building a cohesive union and at the same time reinforcing the principle of subsidiarity. it is worth emphasising that this regulation, although it does not contain any decisions on financial matters, is part of the cohesion policy package, since it is based on treaty provisions on the creation of forms that serve the use of the structural funds or on activities without the use of the structural funds. as rapporteur, i am aware of the many questions and doubts that have been raised in the work on this instrument. as is usual, this is the case when we are dealing with a new instrument, which has not yet been tested and has not yet been given its equivalent in the current legal forms. however, i believe that in this case the codecision procedure will allow us to develop a position which will strengthen the existing crossborder activities and will allow us to achieve significant european added value. author of the draft opinion search by responsible committee . mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. we are all fully aware that the range of objectives we set ourselves and the range of needs we have are far wider and richer than the funds we are able to provide. it is therefore obvious that these funds must be programmed as well as used as efficiently as possible, and this is the direction of the changes proposed for the nearest financial perspective. it is incomprehensible to abandon certain rules that have worked and have worked well so far, and i am thinking here of the principle of multi-funding, which allows the member states to pool the funds needed to carry out a single task in the best possible way, that is to say, to use the money as they see fit in their own country. this solution is to be changed by limiting cross-financing to 5%. why change a rule that works well, for which the administrative instruments have already been built and the staff has been prepared? on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i also want to thank all the authors of the reports in question. the current debate on the future of cohesion policy is a great test of the practical application of one of the fundamental values of the european union - solidarity for equality of opportunity. i would like to remind you that the aim of cohesion policy is to support the restructuring and modernisation of those countries which, without support, have no chance of quickly catching up with the average level of economic development in the european union. today, these are mainly the new member states. from their point of view, the most important issues we are discussing today are certainly the application of the n+2 principle and the eligibility of vat as eligible costs. the nature of projects financed by the cohesion fund means that their preparation itself takes more than two years. these are often large investment projects which deviate from the normal timeframe of projects financed by the structural funds. the extension of the n+2 principle will certainly reduce the level of use of the funds allocated. as regards vat, the experience of the new countries has shown that the main barrier to the use of structural aid is the relatively high start-up costs of projects, borne by the beneficiaries' own resources. the exclusion of vat from the list of eligible costs will mean that many entities, including the local government unit, will not be able to bear these heavy burdens of project implementation. preliminary estimates indicate that, for example, the share of national resources needed to implement projects in the case of the european regional development fund may amount to almost 63% of the value of the union funds. this puts the new member states in a disadvantageous position compared with those which have previously benefited from structural assistance. i appeal to my colleagues from the old member states: let us seize the opportunity to be solidarity, let us give europe a chance to develop, it is also in your interest.

the next item is the report by mrs wallis, drawn up on behalf of the committee on legal affairs, on the draft regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the law applicable to non-contractual obligations (rome ii) (com (2003) 0427 - c5-0338/2003 - 2003/0168 (cod)) (a6-0211/2005)
vice-chairman of the commission . mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, the commission has proposed a compensation initiative which has three objectives. the first objective is to determine solutions in advance and thus to provide legal certainty to citizens and economic operators who are victims of harmful actions. the second objective is to facilitate the settlement of disputes before the courts and to promote mutual recognition of judgments. the third objective is, of course, to facilitate the settlement of such disputes as much as possible. in order to achieve these objectives, we have proposed a general rule, namely the rule of the application of the place where the damage was caused, that is to say the place of direct damage. we have decided to adopt this approach because it is the most widespread solution in the member states' legal systems and also the most balanced solution between the parties in our view. the commission proposal also contained some special rules, such as liability for defective products or for damage to the environment. i believe that in these particular matters the general rule does not always allow a proper balance to be struck, and that special provisions are therefore needed. the initiative provides for a degree of flexibility for judges to allow them to take account of exceptional circumstances. however, this flexibility must be limited in order to avoid compromising the overall objective of legal certainty. in this respect, it is clear that a total discretion of the judiciary would make it difficult to pre-determine the legal certainty which is one of the main objectives of this initiative, since economic operators and citizens want to know in advance which law will be applicable to their situation. in the light of the above, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on her high quality report, the result of very thorough consultation, and i would like to thank her for her determination to proceed swiftly so that the report can be adopted before the summer. the only problem, in my view, is the excessive flexibility afforded to judges in the rapporteur's amendments, in order to allow them to take account of particular circumstances on a case-by-case basis. this excessive discretion is likely to undermine the objective certainty of legal situations. we also have difficulty accepting amendments which abolish the special rules. i referred to liability for defective products, which provides for full consumer protection, or environmental liability. in my view, it would be dangerous to eliminate these special rules. i fully agree with the rapporteur's solution to sensitive issues such as defamation in the press and the relationship between private international law and the internal market. these are two very sensitive areas and i think the compromise reached is satisfactory. in conclusion, as regards road traffic damage, i would like to congratulate mr wallis once again on having thoroughly studied this matter of great practical importance to the citizens. the commission shares our intention to continue a very thorough analysis, for example in the context of the application of the so-called 'rome ii' programme.
draft opinion of the libe committee, drawn up by the author. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. first of all, like the commissioner, i would like to thank mrs wallis very warmly for her very insightful report and for the compromise she has made on many difficult issues. this regulation, although difficult and technical, represents another very important step in the creation of a coherent european civil law system, without which the functioning of the common market is much more difficult, a common market which is sometimes criticised as the basis of european integration. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the libe committee, because of the short time-limit for its work and, above all, the scope of its competence, concentrated primarily on article 6 of that regulation. this article concerns the identification of the law applicable in the event of defamation of good name and reputation, i.e. the defamation of a person or company by a media publication, and the application of this law in any legal dispute. in the opinion of the libe committee, where i was rapporteur, we agreed that the european union must guarantee its citizens a high level of legal certainty. therefore, in the event of a breach of good repute or publicity, it is essential that the rights of the individual victim be protected first and foremost in the country where the damage has been caused. we have started from the assumption that there is no current threat to media freedom in europe, because these freedoms are protected by both the constitutional order of the member states and by the european courts. in addition, as a result of a compromise in the legal affairs committee, an amendment was tabled which, on the one hand, takes account of the libe commission's position and, on the other, creates a legal framework so precise that european publishers should feel satisfied. commissioner. it is very important, because i share your concerns. i firmly believe that strengthening democracy and supporting independent information sources in belarus are of the utmost importance, especially in view of the forthcoming presidential elections. the european commission has a strong interest in belarus being a democratic and stable neighbour and hopefully, in the future, being able to benefit fully from the european neighbourhood policy. recent developments in belarus, however, have moved the country’s political system further away from a european democratic system and norms and values, preventing the country from taking its rightful place in the family of european nations. after the parliamentary elections and the referendum in belarus last year, which fell significantly short of international standards for democratic elections, in november 2004 the council of the european union confirmed the restrictions on ministerial-level contacts with the belarusian authorities. at the same time, the european union sent a very clear message to the population to tell them that we had not forgotten them and that we wanted to enhance contacts with civil society. the european union has consistently condemned the arrests and politically motivated trials of potential opponents to president lukashenko. we have called for respect for the rule of law and the immediate release of these people. we see these actions by the regime as attempts to eliminate opposition leaders, especially in the run-up to the presidential elections in 2006. the growing repression of political parties, non-governmental organisations and independent media outlets is of serious concern to us. we are also closely monitoring the human rights situation in belarus. as a clear signal that the european union cannot accept violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms, last year we imposed a visa ban on certain high-ranking belarusian officials on the basis of council of europe findings. there was the pourgourides report on politically motivated disappearances. we then extended this visa ban to cover the officials considered responsible for rigged elections and also the rigged referendum, as well as those responsible for the repression of peaceful demonstrations. our grave concerns about the observance of trade union rights in belarus have led to an investigation into alleged violations of freedom of association and also the right to collective bargaining, as defined in the ilo conventions, especially within the framework of the gsp, the generalised system of preferences. the investigation might ultimately result in the withdrawal of belarus’s access to the benefits of the gsp. against the background of the worsening political situation in belarus, the european union remains very committed to assisting civil society and the people of belarus. here it must be said that the commission is a major donor to belarus and in the past few months we have also streamlined our assistance to the country. a workshop was organised in vilnius specifically to coordinate our assistance. this was very important, as it gave us the chance to intensify our institutions and the rule of law. this is being done through the eidhr – the european initiative for democracy and human rights – and the decentralised cooperation instrument. two calls for tender were launched there in march and the project selection has already been completed. contracting will probably take place over the summer, so that the activities can start before the end of the year. there are 10 to 12 projects relating to education and advocacy ngos giving legal advice to people who have human rights problems. i hope that the results will be excellent. the second objective is to support the broader needs of the population in related areas. by broader needs, i mean the tacis programme that focuses on support for the population itself in different sectors, including good governance, sustainable development, the social sector, education, health, the environment and economic development, and also alleviation of the problems caused by the chernobyl catastrophe, which figures prominently on our assistance programme. the idea of supporting independent radio broadcasting to belarus has been suggested as an effective and useful response to the lack of alternative and independent information in belarus. we have studied the possibilities carefully and will see how that can be managed. under our current financial regulations it is not easy to find the right solution immediately. however, i can tell you that, as regards the difficulties journalists are facing in belarus, we have a key programme for training journalists and we have already been able to do a lot. we have provided support for the belarusian association of journalists, for which it is very grateful. for instance, we gave it our backing as the winner of the sakharov prize for freedom of thought in 2004.
