in writing. as one of the few meps i voted against the proposal to reject the draft so-called patentability of computer-implemented inventions directive. parliament was given the opportunity to express its views on the draft text through the codecision process. the almost unanimous decision of parliament to reject the project is just (not entirely responsible) decision avoidance. the broad coalition of mps was made up of very different factions. after much thought, i found myself in neither. the opponents of effective protection of intellectual property as such (the far left) voted against the directive. i'm not one of them. opponents of the european system of such protection (the far right) voted against. and i don't share that view. in many countries, it is expensive to register inventions. opponents of extending parliament's political influence over the legislative process (present in each club) voted against. i don't share that view. in the end, all those who considered that the draft directive threatened polish national interests (polish meps) voted against it. apart from the unlimited possibility of change, this is a false assumption. patent protection - broad or narrow - encourages private investment in innovation and hence the employment of researchers. europe has almost twice the rate of such expenditure as the usa. one important reason is the country's extensive patent protection, often cited as a bad example and a scarecrow in this debate.

president-in-office of the council. mr president, i am delighted to be here at the european parliament at the start of the british presidency of the european union. the next six months will be a the road to europe. next week – as recognised by the title of this debate – marks the tenth anniversary of the massacre at srebrenica in july 1995. seven to eight thousand muslim men and women were killed in cold blood in the worst act of genocide in europe since 1945. we recognise that the international community failed to realise what was happening until it was too late and failed in its duty to protect innocent civilians, unarmed men, women and children. however, whatever the sins of omission of the international community, which we deeply regret at this time of sadness and remembrance, let us not forget the sins of commission by the attacking bosnian serb forces. the ultimate responsibility lies with those who murdered, raped and tortured in cold blood. as we all know, some have already been tried and found guilty of their part in these atrocities, others have been acquitted. but those held most responsible – ratko mladic and radovan karadzic – are still at large as fugitives from justice. ten years on from this terrible event, it is surely time for the authorities in the region – in serbia and montenegro, in bosnia and herzegovina, and in croatia – to grasp the nettle and dark days of the early 1990s seem predominantly to be a distant memory. but as we move further down the road to closer integration between the western balkan countries and the european union, it is up member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your contributions to the debate. let me respond to a number of important points that have been raised. first of all, i would like to reiterate that the main purpose of this fundamental change is to give member states greater flexibility to take better account of the needs of the outermost regions. as regards the reference period, and i refer in this connection to the speeches by mr freitas and mr fernandes, some of you are calling for a flexible period for the calculation of the financial ceilings applicable to the specific supply arrangements. i think i can say that the commission has made a considerable effort to ensure that the new aid scheme is favourable to the outermost regions. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the proposal is a package: we cannot extract the good provisions and ask for a review of those which are considered less favourable. i would like to draw your attention to this aspect of my reply. the financial envelopes were calculated on a basis favourable to these regions, in particular because the ceilings for aid to local production were taken into account and not the historical figures. the commission is not prepared to change its proposal on these financial ceilings. as regards the limitation of the specific supply arrangements to agricultural products, both mr freitas and mr casaca have spoken on this point. the commission also wishes to provide a clearer framework for the posei measures. for this reason, the new regime concerns only agricultural products, which are listed in annex i to the treaty. the unsatisfactory situations of the past regarding the management of posei measures should be put to an end. the commission proposes transitional periods to enable the various sectors to adapt to the new situation. the azores and sinaga were also discussed. this issue, raised by mr freitas and mr fernandes, concerns the specific problems of the azores, in particular the sinaga sugar factory. the draft council regulation does not contain any new provisions concerning exports and shipments of products which have benefited from the specific supply arrangements. since 1992, the commission has applied the same criteria for all the outermost regions, i.e. the average of trade flows during the period 1989-1991. this approach was confirmed by the european court of justice in the sinaga case. we have to call him back. the possibilities for financial aid for sugar production in the azores have been considerably strengthened in the draft council regulation. the proposal provides for a financial envelope for aid to local production, calculated on the basis of the potential for developing sugar production within the framework of production quotas, of almost eur 4 million per year, instead of the current actual production of eur 400 million per year. on the basis of this generous envelope and within the framework of the wide margin of flexibility left to member states in choosing the sectors to be subsidised, it is for the national authorities to decide to increase the aid to sugar production and to the specified sugar factory, if they so wish, after consulting all interested parties. the commission is convinced that these new rules will improve the framework for these schemes, first and foremost in the interests of the outermost regions.

the next item is the debate on the recommendation for second reading by the committee on employment and social affairs on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the minimum health and safety requirements regarding the exposure of workers to the risks arising from physical agents (optical radiation) (nineteenth individual directive within the meaning of article 16 (1) of directive 89/391/eec) (05571/6/2005 - c6-0129/2005 - 1992/0449 ((cod)) (rapporteur: csaba őry) (a6-0249/2005).
the commission's vice-president mr president, the commission and the council are aware that prevention of natural hazards must be treated differently and the common position reflects this difference. i shall therefore, mr president, explain the commission's position on the amendments. i would like to begin by thanking parliament for the work it has done and for the debate it has had. during the long and difficult legislative process, the commission has been keen to do its utmost to maintain a high level of protection for workers in this text, avoiding discrimination between workers exposed to risks with similar consequences, in compliance with the provisions of framework directive 89/391, while ensuring the necessary proportionality. this is to allow, at the end of the process, a compromise acceptable to all the institutions concerned. the commission cannot therefore accept what is being said, in particular in some media, that the text of the common position is a useless exercise, conducive to giving the european citizen a bureaucratic and sterile image of the european union. the commission believes that the common position is a balanced text which responds to the real dangers of eye diseases and skin cancers - melanoma - faced by all citizens and is perfectly in line with the terms of the recent european parliament resolution on the promotion of health and safety. we must of course find ways of avoiding unnecessary burdens on our businesses, and in particular, as many have pointed out, on small and mediumsized enterprises. amendments nos 1, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 36 reinforce the need for early detection of health effects and specify the level of qualification of those responsible for medical surveillance. the commission may accept them. the commission can also accept amendments nos 2, 3, 6, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 34 and 35. they improve the text and reinforce and clarify the meaning of the provision concerned. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 5, 7 and 37 as they stand, which propose to leave it to each member state to legislate on whether or not employers should carry out a risk assessment in the case of exposure to radiation of natural origin. in addition to the considerations of protecting the health of workers, referred to above, such provisions would be contrary to the obligations imposed on employers by framework directive 89/391 to take account of all risks and to carry out a risk assessment in all cases. the adoption of these amendments - i stress this point a little, mr president, because it is an important point of law - would in a way involve a transfer of responsibility from the employer to the national legislator. i believe that this would pose a real problem in terms of labour law and working conditions and would not, in my view, make the task of the states any easier. i therefore insist on this point. similarly, amendment no 18 in favour of rejecting the common position, amendments nos 21 and 24, which exclude in particular the inclusion of particularly sensitive risk groups or effects due to interactions with photosensitizing substances, and all amendments nos 19 to 23, 25 to 33, which exclude optical radiation of natural origin from the scope of the directive, cannot be accepted by the commission, even though it understands the reasons which may have led to these amendments. the commission intends to work with parliament and the council to find a solution which will allow the directive to be adopted as soon as possible. as regards amendments nos 4 and 13, which introduce a provision requiring the commission to draw up a guide to good practice, the commission is prepared to consider how best to respond to them, while remaining concerned to avoid procedures which would undermine the drafting quality of community legislation governed by an interinstitutional agreement. the commission hopes that the amendments which will be adopted tomorrow will enable the text of the new directive to achieve fully the objectives of article 137 of the treaty in the field of workers' health and social security. i would like to emphasize the quality of the compromise reached, by differentiating the risks according to their origin and by simply authorizing, i believe, particularly for natural hazards, a number of precautionary measures which can simply be reminded to workers in the interests of their health and which thus complement the provisions for protecting the health of workers in europe, without going into too much detail and complication. that is why i think that this compromise, mr president, really deserves the full attention of parliament.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the line between tv, the internet and telephony is blurring. it creates new challenges. the legal acts that we have in the european union, at the european level, do not respond to these challenges, including in terms of protecting the mental and moral development of the youngest media users. the first major problem is the removal of responsibility from the member state for the content of programmes broadcast from abroad. the category of border state or union of states is anachronistic in the media world and not reacting to program content just because it is broadcast from abroad is irresponsible. the technical safeguards required for content that threatens the moral development of children are outdated and ineffective today. they are now only serving to improve the well-being of those who introduced them into the directive. we also forget that in addition to the content that should not normally be available to children, we have in article 22 categories of programmes that should not be broadcast at all. 'the content of the programme should not be obscene or pornographic', the directive says. 'the broadcasting of programmes which endanger the mental and emotional development of children is also prohibited', the directive continues. at the same time, we are unable to deal with the problem of delivering harmful content in software packages to families who do not want it. we are, of course, at odds with the fundamental principle of free speech, and it is we, not the porn industry, who are being defeated. it's unfortunate that this simple clash of norms cannot be resolved in the interest of common sense and the public good. the large number of derogations and exceptions in the directive leads the member states and the european union itself to fail to apply the directive, in particular article 22. an example is the european commission's inaction in relation to a complaint about the registration of a pornographic channel by the french national audiovisual council. this registration is not only a violation of the directive in france, but is also the basis for applying for the automatic introduction of this channel, for example in poland. this is not what the possibility of greater protection for the viewer under national law should look like. the report by marielle de sarnez is a good response to all these challenges, to all these problems, and therefore deserves our support. however, it cannot be ignored that the frequent reference to the dead draft of the constitutional treaty in this document significantly weakens it.
mr. chairman, please! we all welcome the draft paediatric regulation as an expression of concern for children's health in europe and beyond. however, it should be borne in mind that this regulation will have a greater negative financial impact on some countries than on others. mr verheugen, as a former commissioner for enlargement, you are probably better acquainted than anyone else with the difficult financial situation of the health sector in poland. excessively long periods of patent protection and registration data protection would be particularly disastrous for poorer countries, where the market economy system guaranteeing a normal functioning economy has only recently been established. let us work together to ensure that the pharmaceutical industry, which does not complain about the lack of revenue, does not use too much of the money of the societies of our member states. i am in favour of minimum bonuses for the pharmaceutical sector and the possibility of generic medicines as soon as possible. however, as ms roth-behrendt points out in her final report, the quality of child health care is more important than the savings made.
mr. chairman, please! the regulation on medicinal products for paediatric use is needed by everyone, and especially by children the youngest citizens of the european union. it's about providing better medicine at affordable prices, at prices that every mother can afford. i want to congratulate your rapporteur on her work on this document. with this regulation, we are sending a good signal to our voters, we are showing that parliament supports the work on the development of paediatric medicines, cares about the medical conditions of our children, cares about their health. however, we made a number of mistakes in drafting this regulation. fortunately, we still have a chance to eliminate them in the vote tomorrow. firstly, i am against the so-called 'prize pooling', i.e. the granting of financial support for the same research or for the same investments. secondly, i consider it wrong to abolish the obligation to register a paediatric medicinal product in all member states as a condition for obtaining additional patent protection. paediatric medicines should be registered and available in all countries, not just in some countries. i do not agree that some eu citizens should be denied access to new and better medicines, and yet the company that makes them should be rewarded. it's socially unfair, legally unjustified and against the principle of equality. the european parliament should not accept this. thirdly, i have serious reservations about the proposal to extend patent protection for paediatric medicines, since a patent protects any new medicine, whether it is used to treat a child, a woman or an elderly person. there is no doubt that extending patent protection will limit access to the generic market. we shouldn't have agreed to this. every mother will pay any price for the health of her child, but i want to ask: why should she pay more when, by passing the amendments, parliament can give her a chance to pay as much as she needs to?

author of the draft opinion of the cult committee. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the draft resolution of the european parliament on new prospects and new challenges for sustainable european tourism has attracted considerable interest from the committee on culture and education. the commission has delivered an opinion to the committee on transport and tourism, drawing particular attention to: the need to focus on long-term tourism in its various aspects (i.e. economic, cultural, natural and social) and the need to value seasonal tourism, the link between tourism development and the protection of national, regional and local culture, as well as the natural environment, parks, landscapes, urban planning, architectural ensembles and objects, the use of tourism for economic development, job creation and the preservation of human physical and mental health, the proper management of tourism resources, the development of agro-tourism (particularly in the new member states) and the education of young people in the field of cultural, sporting, sporting, sporting and cultural activities. the majority of these proposals were adopted by the committee on transport and tourism and incorporated into the final draft resolution. the result is an interesting document which, although dominated by organisational and economic issues, notes the timeless values, including culture, nature, the natural environment of man. the draft resolution omitted or under-emphasised qualified tourism, the protection of historic cities, architectural ensembles and objects and the european cultural tourism card. these issues will need to be given more attention in future work on sustainable tourism development.
mr. chairman, please! it is of course true that tourism is not directly subject to european community legislation. there is another truth that luis queiroz's report makes clear. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the establishment of a european network of information centres, the establishment of a european network of information centres and the establishment of a european network of information centres. there were many arguments in favour of this in the debate today. i would like to mention one more, which i think is not the least important. well, tourism is also about people communicating. the tourist not only gets to know the sights and attractions, but also new people, previously unknown to him. in the process of these contacts, prejudices, negative stereotypes, bad historical past are weakened and collapsed. in fact, only direct contact with another human being can change these attitudes. when we make contact with each other, we stop being strangers. how important this is in the context of the enlarged european union, especially for young people. i therefore propose that, following the example of socrates and erasmus, tourism programmes for young people be developed. let's give them the chance to see europe from spain to estonia and from sweden to malta and cyprus. to get to know each other so we can understand each other much better than we have in the past. i think it's worth working on these programs, not sparing time or money.
mr. chairman, please! tourism is a journey, it's a wander. a traveler has always been someone who sets out to see the world, to learn something, to come back richer in experience and skill. he was going through universities all over europe. this is how a european identity was built, a european consciousness of values, a europe of universities, of cathedrals, of great artists and craftsmen. today, tourism is more about the pursuit of quick, consuming pleasure. to this day, i often quote the motto on the école du ski français: 'pleasure is something you learn' (le plaisire ça s'apprend). we can appreciate the value of a skill or knowledge only if we put forth the effort to do so. unfortunately, today's tourism is like the supermarkets scattered all over europe. it's dominated by the same goal: to make space cheap, easily accessible, and ideally, most of it the same. the movement has been lightning fast. we're running out of time, so we're swallowing more tourist products. the tourism industry is adapting. sell a colorful picture of the sea, the mountains and the pool. it is often said that tourism creates jobs, but at what cost? a mindless record-breaking visit. the one with the most million hits is the one with the most hits. this report is therefore important because europe must focus on the quality of tourism, it must take up the challenge of mass tourism, especially as it now supports the development of regional airports and low-cost airlines. we need to restore the meaning of the word travel, wandering. we need to create educational programs that prevent the destruction of the natural environment and the historical heritage. new initiatives for sustainable tourism are needed. remembering that the love of world heritage, nature or the supermaterial leads through the recognition of the value of the world that surrounds us the small homeland of each of us. mr. chairman, please! a series of recent scandals, such as those involving enron and parlamat, have weakened the confidence of investors as well as consumers. the scale of these scandals was alarming and they involved all kinds of fraud. in this situation, the commission's initiative is most welcome. the commission's draft legislative inquiry is the result of many years of preparation, taking into account the recommendations of 2000 and 2002. this directive will replace the 8th directive on statutory auditors of 1984, which only contains rules on the accreditation of auditors but does not mention an audit, supervision or external quality control procedure. the draft new directive clearly defines the tasks of statutory auditors and lays down certain ethical principles to ensure their professionalism and independence, i.e. integrity, objectivity, professional competence, confidentiality and professional secrecy and general responsibility. the commission's proposal on the principle of rotation between firm and partner was one of the most controversial issues that aroused the most emotion. the rotation principle is generally to be welcomed as it ensures independence and promotes objective assessment. the downsides of rotation are the extra costs, the loss of know-how and, therefore, the risk of error. the audit firm should change at least every seven years and the interval between assignments should be at least two years. a balance needs to be struck between reducing the risk of fraud, ensuring healthy competition and a high level of service quality. the approach presented in the report appears to be a balanced and reasonable solution to the issue of assuring audit quality while ensuring the independence of the auditor. in conclusion, i would like to stress that our aim should be to restore confidence in the market, as well as to strengthen shareholder rights, investment security and the competitiveness of european companies.
member of the commission. mr president, i would like to start by thanking all the speakers for their remarks. i would like to comment on a number of points, beginning with the one raised by mrs fraga concerning licence fees. the rebalancing of costs is not something which is new. if one looks at the evolution of this since the mid-1980s, one finds that until the mid-1990s the share ratio was 80:20. then, from the mid 1990s up to the present day, the share ratio changed to 75:25. we are introducing a new sharing of costs of 65:35. i can say that the commission's decision to increase the tuna fee paid by shipowners is justified in several respects, including the need to increase the financial responsibility of ec shipowners and guarantee a fair contribution for the coastal state. as indicated in the council's conclusions of july 2004, this contribution must be fair, balanced and non-discriminatory. the 35:65 share is already applied in all the tuna agreements concluded in the pacific, including kiribati and the solomon islands and the federated states of micronesia, and the member states concerned did not object to this. by the time of the renewal of the ec-seychelles protocol last september the commission had already announced to the council's external group that it intended to adopt the 35:65 ratio. during negotiations, the seychelles asked the commission to delay this change in order to avoid distortion of competition with the tanzania agreement, which is soon to enter into force and under the initial phase of which the applicable ratio will still be 25:75. the ec/seychelles agreement therefore maintained the 25:75 ratio, but a formula was agreed under which the transition to the 35:65 ratio will take effect in the near future. harmonisation of the 35:65 ratio in other fisheries agreements will be introduced in 2006. the same 35:65 ratio will be introduced in the other fisheries agreements in the area, those with mauritius and madagascar, which will be negotiated in 2006. in addition, the commission intends to hold a meeting with the tuna sector by the end of 2005, to discuss all relevant issues. i also underline and repeat that there is constant dialogue with the sector, within the framework of the special sectoral group, and i will see to it that this dialogue is further intensified. i will also see what can be done to minimise as far as possible the delays in making payments to third parties. on the point raised by mrs corbey, may i point out that all agreements are undertaken further to an assessment of the health of fish stocks. let me cite the recent morocco agreement, where the commission showed how seriously it takes its obligations by first undertaking a scientific assessment, in accordance with the new policy for the fisheries partnership agreements. the agreement was then targeted on what one may term 'the excess stock'. in other words, the fish that can be caught sustainably, beyond what local fishermen can themselves catch. so the agreement only covers that excess stock of fish within the limits of sustainability. this policy is being adopted and applied to all fishery partnership agreements. i thank mr schlyter for his support with regard to the rebalancing of the costs. i also thank mr medina ortega for his support with regard to the new partnership agreement on fisheries and i will see to it that everything is done to limit unnecessary red tape. i would also like to thank him for the insights stemming from his direct experience of fisheries in the comoros and the indian ocean. in reply to mrs goudin, this agreement envisages a development segment under which the union not only benefits from fishing rights but is obliged to assist in the fisheries sector of the comoros. this is a new element of the partnership agreements which is being introduced to all agreements with third countries.

european regions. this does not mean, of course, that the development of europe's strongest and most dynamic regions is being weakened, but on the contrary: it means that the development potential of the weakest regions is being increased and their chances of becoming competitive are being increased. the recent enlargement of the european union, as well as the enlargements to follow, have given the european union new challenges, including the need to adapt cohesion policy to new conditions and challenges. the new conditions that have arisen in the enlarged european union require that the existing measures for social and economic cohesion be extended to include horizontal measures, with greater emphasis on the need to reduce disparities between the centre and the periphery, between metropolitan areas and medium-sized and small towns, and between towns and rural areas. the new conditions also require that the disparities between the above communities be addressed with greater have condemned firmly the acts of intimidation by the belarusian authorities against the union of the poles in belarus. these incidents occur in the context of growing repression of political parties, ngos and independent media outlets in belarus. we believe such interference undermines minority rights, thereby contravening standards of governance to which belarus has signed up as part of its commitments to the organisation of security and cooperation in europe. in addition, belarus has introduced decrees that place even more restrictions on foreign assistance, thereby isolating itself and the belarusian people still further. you may ask how the commission has reacted. in response to the growing repression in belarus we have increased our funding for democratisation and human rights by transferring eur 2 million from the tacis programme to the european initiative for democracy and human rights programme, one of the two instruments which do not require the consent of the government. the tacis programme was refocused to address the needs of the population with the full participation of the civil society. this year we have already signed 27 small contracts with ngos worth eur 3 million. we shall issue a further call for proposals under the eidhr programme in october, with a total budget of eur 420 000. we are also in the process of allocating more than eur 1.7 million for three specific new projects for belarus. these will be implemented by osce - odihr, the undp and the nordic council of ministers. these projects will focus on human rights, democratisation, civil society and independent educational institutions such as the european humanities university-in-exile. we shall continue to address the broader needs of the population with the tacis programme and focus on health and social issues, higher education, training and environmental matters. when alleviating chernobyl-related problems, our approach is to fund project proposals put forward by the local communities. one of the most significant developments in our assistance is our support for independent broadcasting. in response to the suggestions from this parliament and elsewhere, starting from 1 november we shall fund a daily radio news programme. the idea is to increase awareness of human rights and democracy issues in the belarusian population, and provide it with factual news on developments inside and outside belarus, which would not otherwise be available. the broadcasting will kick off in russian, and belarusian programmes will be phased in as soon as possible. the start of independent broadcasting is a major step, and i am delighted that we were the first donor to launch such initiatives for belarus. in addition, we shall open a commission office in minsk early next year. the office will be headed by a chargé d'affaires. this will facilitate our contacts with local civil society and it will also assist our coordination efforts and the follow-up of our activities. we have also looked at how best to ensure that all our policies towards belarus are consistent and coherent. in trade we have carried out an investigation into violations of trade union rights under the generalised system of preferences and looked into the definition of annual textiles quotas. we also keep the eu list of senior officials covered by the visa ban under continual review. the march, followed by one in kiev in july, and the latest one was held last week in brussels. the process of democratisation in belarus and the wellbeing of its people are matters that are very close to mr. chairman, please! energy from renewable sources should be used in accordance with the technological priorities of the country. in poland, the climate and agricultural conditions make biofuels a priority requiring rapid support, with geothermal energy in second place. however, the experience so far with solid biomass electricity generation is not very optimistic. this is due to, inter alia, the low efficiency of heat-to-electric conversion, as well as logistical and environmental problems. in addition, biomass for wood products must be dried by evaporating about 20% of the water, which consumes additional energy. another priority for poland could be the energy contained in municipal waste, whose sources are not only renewable but are increasing rapidly and alarmingly. so it's by definition a renewable energy source. existing technologies, including pyrolysis, make it possible to extract hydrocarbons from waste and convert them into electricity at high efficiency. the two-fold effect is achieved: energy and a kind of secondary recycling and the elimination of landfills. the commission should recognise this type of energy as renewable.

member of the commission. madam president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr chmielewski, and the committee on fisheries for the report on the commission’s proposal for technical measures in the baltic sea. i must express my gratitude for the open attitude taken by the committee and the rapporteur, in particular to the arguments put forward by the commission, resulting in a report which the commission can accept almost in its entirety. this is a very technical file and, as you are aware, technical conservation measures in the baltic sea presently originate in large part from fisheries rules adopted at international level in the international baltic sea fisheries committee – ibsfc. the community has adopted some additional rules for its own waters, which now cover all of the baltic sea except for the two small portions of russian waters. in community legislation, the measures are spread out in three different council regulations: the baltic technical measures regulation, the regulation on industrial fishing for herring – both from 1998 – and the annual tac and quota regulation, which also contains a number of technical conservation measures. apart from this legal complexity, the present rules are, in some cases, over-complicated and, in others, unclear and remain open to interpretation. they are therefore difficult to implement and to control. on 14 march 2005, the commission adopted a proposal for a new regulation on technical conservation measures for the baltic sea. the proposal was drafted after extensive consultation with the baltic stakeholders and the member states during 2004. it groups together all the relevant rules into a single legislative act, which will improve legal consistency. furthermore, the proposal seeks to simplify and to streamline the rules as far as possible by, for example, proposing uniform closed seasons for certain species instead of having differing time periods in different parts of the baltic. the consultation held within the committee on fisheries was characterised by a spirit of good cooperation, which has led to a strong result. the commission’s proposal is very technical with many details relating to the construction and use of fishing gear in the baltic. i am very pleased that the rapporteur and the committee on fisheries have been able to address the very technical elements of the proposal and have come forward with a number of amendments which will improve the proposal. amendments 5 and 6 are a good example of this. strict rules were proposed for all the nets comprising the trawl to guarantee its efficient selectivity. these amendments allow the reduction of the application of the strict rules to the rear part of the trawl. thus, the selectivity of the fishing gear is not affected. the rules have been simplified and are easier to understand for the fishermen, and control at sea is facilitated. i can support all but one of the 15 amendments proposed in the report. the only amendment on which i have reservations is amendment 3. if we accept that fisheries inspectors can only take samples of a landing if the sample has been accepted by the ship owner, we may undermine the inspectors’ ability to carry out the necessary controls. furthermore, i must remind you that it is always up to the inspectors to prove that the samples they have taken are representative of the landing. therefore, i am not in a position to support the adoption of amendment 3. i can accept amendment 9, on the introduction of an assessment of the effects of driftnets and other entangling gears on the sea mammal populations. however, let me make it clear that i am not prepared to accept the modification of the phasing-out of driftnets, as already adopted by the council with parliament’s support, in 2004. let me finish by once again thanking the rapporteur and the committee for their excellent work.
the rapporteur. - madam president! - i have to go. the council regulation of 14 march on the conservation of fishery resources in the baltic sea by technical measures, which is the subject of my report, joins a long line of eu documents which aim, on the one hand, to codify the solutions already in place and, on the other, to extend their scope to the new ten, four of which are known to be baltic states. not everyone, let us say at once, liked the new four in the council's proposal. many of the articles that were relevant were rejected. the rapporteur, who comes from one of these countries, and who is thus one of the main addressees of the new directives, has been faced with a difficult political conundrum and a difficult challenge. the aim was, of course, as usual, to find a favourable compromise, a compromise all the more difficult to achieve since it concerned a subject which is not easily amenable to mediation, namely technical fishing measures. and the technique of fishing, beyond the political intent, is simply subject to daily practical verification by the human, the fisherman, and the indifferent to the political mediating spells of the fish. fortunately, and i thank the members and commissioners who have been involved in this work, the debate has been reduced to a few key points. the main achievement was to find a compromise solution to the problem of fishing gear for cod, the baltic's most important fish, which is the main source of livelihood for baltic fishermen. in addition to the recommended starting window for young fish, the 'bakoma' type, which is a detail, the european parliament's committee on fisheries and the european commission have agreed to use the polish-german equivalent, already tested and cheaper t90 bag. moreover, the working discussions with the authors of the draft regulation have made it possible to supplement the document with what was simply missing, namely the necessary definitions of the elements of fishing gear referred to in the following articles, and in particular the extension device, which is the most frequently cited and ambiguously understood element in the regulation. this procedure has really cleared up a lot of doubts, freed many of the controversial language, and helped some to extract the flexible message from some articles. this has enabled the rapporteur to withdraw amendment no 16 and to relax his other five amendments, particularly those relating to the restrictive article 6, which is a concern for the baltic fisheries, as the commissioner has said, and which requires the withdrawal of certain fairly commonly used fishing gear. finally, the salmon tuna problem, which has been the subject of the greatest concern in our committee on fisheries of the european parliament. in the opinion of polish fishermen, floats, which are considered in europe as equipment that poses too great a risk, for example when fishing for salmon, for marine mammals, guinea pigs, do not pose such a risk in the southern part of the baltic sea, since guinea pigs are present sporadically. it is also true that the decision to close the fleet will also deprive some 60 polish shipowners of the opportunity to fish for salmon in this part of the baltic. the rapporteur, aware of both aspects of this problem of the baltic's fishing fleet, namely the eu's protection requirements for the baltic's mr. chairman, please! the trend today is to use stem cells to treat various diseases. the use of cells of embryonic origin is unethical and the use of mature cells does not raise such concerns. the former do not bring benefits, while the latter bring many. the former account for about 95% of research funding, the latter for only 5%. what's going on here? on 12 may, professor scolding, a neuroscientist at the university of bristol, gave a very interesting speech to the european parliament's intergroup on bioethics, in which he explained a great many issues on this subject. embryonic cells are carcinogenic, they're genetically altered, they have a rejection problem, they have other functions than repair, so they're forced to do things that are not their normal roles. there is also the problem of ethical concerns. mature bone marrow stem cells have therapeutic functions, and you don't force the cells to do anything other than what they're designed to do. there's no problem with rejection, because your own cells are not carcinogenic, they don't cause genetic changes, there's no ethical problem. the results of all these studies are known not only to professor scolding but to all professionals in the field. why, then, is so much money spent on embryonic research and so little on mature cells? with the latter, there is no potential for drug production. the medicine is taken directly from the patient. the drug companies won't make any money, but with embryos, it's all about growing cell lines for different purposes to sell, hence the research money. these are the consequences of patenting cells.

mr. chairman, please! the first reading of the 2006 budget of the european union is proof that the european parliament, a symbol of diversity - and a place for radical voices such as those we have just heard - is capable of reaching a compromise on difficult budgetary issues. there were over 900 amendments at the beginning, and now we have an agreed strategy that should be confirmed in tomorrow's vote. this was achieved despite the fact that 2006 is a difficult year from a budgetary point of view (for the reasons mentioned), with an accumulation of expenditure that was difficult to predict at the beginning of the current financial perspective. this is a great achievement for the rapporteurs: mr pittelle, mr dombrovskis, the goodwill coordinators of the political groups, the advisers of these groups and, of course, the secretariat, headed by mrs maria fialho. the european parliament thus has a position both on the one-year budget for 2006 and on the financial perspective for 2007-13. unfortunately, that cannot be said of the government side, the council side. we expect positions to be taken on a multiannual basis, and we also expect that the conciliation procedure will not be in vain in november on the 2006 budget. it requires a clear mandate from the government, and it will be a crucial test of the british presidency. the mandate for the 2006 conciliation, that's the test that's going to take place in november of this year. the strategy has already been drawn up by parliament. the interesting part of it is that parliament is confirming its right to participate in 1/5 of administrative expenditure, but it is also starting to look for savings from itself. we respect the interinstitutional agreement, we use its power and also the instrument of flexibility in this interpretation, as confirmed by commissioner grybauskaitė. we know that agreement - agreement on money - is the good news that the citizens of the european union are waiting for.

in writing. title:- regulation of the european parliament and of the council on certain fluorinated greenhouse gases. - and a draft directive of the european parliament and of the council on emissions from certain air-conditioning systems in motor vehicles and amending council directive 70/156/eec. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' in the definition of the term 'competent authority'. mr president, the f-gas regulation is an example of over-regulation that does not fit the reality. why introduce another environmental regulation when statistical analyses show that the harmfulness of f-gases is negligible, even close to statistical error? what we have here is a complete lack of a sustainable approach to environmental and industrial development. it is also alarming that the adoption of a single legal basis for the regulation, i.e. article 95 tec, could cause distortions in the functioning of the common market. poland and other member states which have not restricted the use of f-gases strongly oppose such a decision, claiming that the regulation is based on two legal bases (i.e. articles 95 and 175 tec). this would aim to introduce uniform requirements throughout the european union for restrictions and prohibitions on the placing on the single market of certain products containing f-gases. the principle of the common market would thus not be infringed. there is no doubt that the effects of the reduction of fluorinated gases will be disproportionate in economic terms in most of the new member states to the environmental effect.

madam president! i would like to express my gratitude to the afghan people and the afghan authorities, in particular to president karzai, for holding free elections, which represent one of the essential steps towards building democracy and peace in afghanistan. the elections on september 18 this year saw 5,700 candidates, including 575 women. elections were held for the wolesi jirga, the lower house of the national assembly, and for the provincial councils. to give you an idea of the scale of the problem, consider that 26,000 polling stations were set up across the country, and in kabul itself, for example, the ballot paper had seven pages, with 617 names on it for 62 seats in the constituency. 30% of the seats in the wolesi jirga and the provincial councils are reserved for women. while more than 3 million women voted in the 2004 presidential election, more than 7,000 new women registered to vote in this year's election, representing 44% of all new voters. this is just the beginning of afghan democracy. the european parliament's mission to afghanistan ahead of the elections, led by mr brok of the committee on foreign affairs and mrs morgantini of the committee on development, met candidates, women's organisations, human rights groups and ngos in kabul, herat and bâmiân on 14-19 july. we were faced with the hopes for democracy's victory, as well as the threats to that process. i would put the security of the country, violence against women and corruption among the main threats. many former military leaders accused of human rights violations and even crimes participated in the elections and were elected. there is also a risk that afghan politics will be influenced by criminal elements, primarily drug lords and traffickers. the european union must do everything possible to stabilise afghan democracy and the country's resurgent civil society.

the author. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. one of the last great lamas of tibet, tenzin delek rinpoche, has been committed to the preservation of tibetan culture for 20 years. as a prominent religious figure in tibet, he was also actively involved in economic, cultural and social activities. the tibetan lama has long been a source of embarrassment to the chinese authorities, despite the fact that he has never participated in political demonstrations. as a spiritual leader who is sincerely committed to important social causes such as building schools for orphans, a hospice, local roads, and also promoting care for the elderly, he is a peaceful authority, with no shadow of aggression in his actions. however, his popularity was seen as a threat to the chinese local authorities, who arrested him on the pretext of alleged complicity in a series of attacks. a man accused of terrorism has been sentenced to death without evidence or due process. he's been held in inhumane conditions for months awaiting execution. as a result of prolonged torture, lama tenzin delek is now in a fatal state of health. in light of the above, we demand that the chinese authorities improve the conditions in which he is being held. we also demand that the chinese government take steps to improve the conditions of detention of prisoners, to abolish torture and, above all, the death penalty. as an international community, we must send a clear signal that we do not condone the incarceration of people who have not been proven guilty. china must respect international human rights standards and respect human dignity and civil liberties. i therefore also call on the international organisations to put pressure on china to finally engage in a constructive dialogue with a view to a final settlement of the tibet problem.

author. – the question jointly submitted by the committee on constitutional affairs and the committee on budgets involves an invitation to the council to enter into serious negotiations on the operating framework for the agencies. i am sure that there is a well-recognised need here in the european union to rationalise and standardise procedures for setting up and operating the regulatory agencies in the interest of transparency and in order to avoid the duplication of tasks and unnecessary expenditure. i am referring in particular to the agencies involved in executive functions, partly with respect to their functions disintegrating the operational responsibility of the european commission. setting up agencies is now a fashionable response to various challenges in the european union. no wonder that there were five of them ten years ago and, by next year, there will be twenty-three. they are mushrooming and have ever greater budgetary implications because this is not only about operational expenditure; this is about expenditure of a more bureaucratic nature. now we have a very good basis for discussion in the commission communication, namely the draft interinstitutional agreement of february 2005. following the white paper on european governance, the european parliament adopted its position in the form of a resolution of january 2004. we, and in particular the budgets committee, understand the significance of applying the principle of budgetary rigour to the setting-up and operation of the agencies, and we fully support the proposal by the temporary committee to ring-fence expenditure on the agencies and to regulate both existing and new agencies. however, that is not in the commission communication. our oral question is in fact an expression of regret that the council is not entering into these negotiations. the major question is whether the council is ready and sees it as necessary and feasible to conclude the negotiations next year, that is, at the end of the current financial perspective.
mr. chairman, please! european regulatory agencies have been established since the 1990s in response to the development of eu policies, successive enlargements and the resulting new technical and scientific needs in the european union. according to the white paper on public governance, the european regulatory agencies contribute to the effective implementation and application of community rules and their functioning and control are of major political and institutional importance. nevertheless, the continued growth in the number of decentralised agencies - now 23 compared with 5 in 1995 - in the absence of a common procedural framework is of concern. the multiplicity of names, tasks, structures and control mechanisms of these agencies creates a situation that is not transparent to the citizen and is detrimental to legal certainty. the european court of auditors' annual report for 2004 reveals shortcomings in the agency's compliance with budgetary rules, staff recruitment and public procurement procedures. in view of the increasing burden that agencies place on the union budget, a thorough analysis of the financial impact of the activities of each newly established agency should be mandatory. in view of the smooth functioning of the union of 25, greater transparency and coherence are necessary in order to avoid the creation of agencies that are increasingly diverse and often duplicate their responsibilities and activities with the relevant services of the european commission. in this context, the draft agreement between the commission, parliament and the council to define common guidelines and a framework for the creation of new regulatory agencies deserves full support. it is also completely incomprehensible that the council has no will to negotiate this agreement, but today i see that it is slowly emerging.

major challenges that we are currently facing. looking at its recent history, the european union has achieved the best progress when deepening and widening, if not hand-in-hand, then at least in parallel. since 1989, since the tearing down of the berlin wall, we have deepened our political integration by creating the single market, the single currency and the schengen arrangement on the free movement of people, and have reinforced the common foreign and security policy. at the same time, the union has widened: our membership has more than doubled from 12 to 25. that parallel deepening and widening proves that it can be done and that it is also beneficial to the european union. in the near future, the continuation of constitutional reform is essential for the european union, in my view, the next item is the debate on - the report by rebecc harms, on behalf of the committee on industry, research and energy, on the proposal for a council regulation implementing protocol no 9 to the act concerning the conditions of accession of the czech republic, estonia, cyprus, latvia, lithuania, hungary, malta, poland, slovenia and slovakia to the european union, on the bohunice v1 nuclear power plant in slovakia (com (2004) 0642 - c6-0205/2004 - 2004/0221cns) (a6-0282/2005) and - the report by rebecc harms, on behalf of the committee on industry, research and energy, on the use of financial resources for the decommissioning of nuclear power plants (2005/2727 (a27/06ini))
member of the commission. mr president, i will start by thanking the rapporteur for her very correct and deep analysis of the challenges concerning decommissioning. as regards the bohunice issue, firstly the decision to close the reactors was based on safety reasons. in the european union, wenra –the western european nuclear regulators’ association – decides on the safety requirements in particular member states. it proposed that those types of reactors were not upgradable, not because they came from the former soviet union, but because of their technical characteristics. that was why the closure of those reactors was requested during the negotiations. that information was known early on, and so the negotiations took into account all the possible consequences. the decision was not taken in the last package: in many cases, including cases in the slovak republic, governments made early commitments to close particular reactors, for example those in bohunice. that is why i reject the argument that political pressure was exerted: the decision was based on the analyses made by those responsible for nuclear safety in the european union. that is a fact. negotiations have been conducted accordingly, and all possible implications have been taken into account, not just decommissioning but other issues too. that is also why we have different protocols for lithuania and slovakia. i realise that decommissioning is a huge task, but i can clearly explain the basis for the commission’s proposal: it was based on the results of the accession negotiations. any other issue should be based on other considerations, but at this stage we are unable to move on to other considerations. my services are in close contact with the slovak authorities to discuss the challenge. however, this is clearly a commitment that was approved by the european union citizens and the slovak citizens in the accession negotiations and it must be honoured, not only from the eu side but also from the slovak side. it is, therefore, a challenge that we should face together. at the same time, there is a question mark over whether decommissioning funds should be used at a time when all the reactors have been operational and are still operational: if you do not have the decommissioning fund, the price is cheaper. but then, at the end of the day, who is paying? taxpayers? other citizens? this really is a global challenge. the debate today, at this late hour, is very relevant. the commission has already tried to make legislative proposals on the decommissioning funds because they are essential for competitiveness inside the european union and for clarifying who will pay for them. i agree entirely that the polluter should pay. that element should be included in the price. the commission will prepare a recommendation and will insist on the sufficient and transparent use of decommissioning funds that should be available when required. that is the basic truth that we should confront when discussing nuclear energy. competition issues definitely will not be excluded from the debate, because it is very important to know what support schemes we are providing for other parts of our energy mix. that is a very relevant issue. i thank you very much for the debate tonight. i am really pleased it was so detailed. we should continue this debate when we discuss energy issues. (applause)

mr. chairman, please! the european parliament will once again present its position on climate change at the un in late november and early december. before it is discussed at international level, it is important that it best reflects the interests of all the member states of the union, including the role of nuclear energy, as mrs grossetête and mr hökmark have rightly said. given that greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise in many member states, full implementation of the un convention and the kyoto protocol will require greater participation of individual citizens in the overall effort to reduce emissions and develop a more sustainable lifestyle. in this context, an important aspect in the fight to reduce co2 emissions is the so-called integrated approach involving politicians, industry and society. an integrated approach is a more efficient and less costly way of reducing co2 emissions. it assumes that the responsibility for reduction lies with both car manufacturers, fuel, and vehicle users. the state of the road infrastructure and traffic management systems is also important. this is in line with the european climate change programme ii announced in october 2005. while moving beyond a fossil-fuel economy is a historic opportunity for entrepreneurship, it is important to remember that many countries - particularly developing countries - have renewable energy resources but do not currently have the technologies to exploit them. energy subsidies are also a major issue in the negotiations on reducing greenhouse gases. there are already many ways to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. energy-efficient and low-emission technologies are an effective means of combating environmental pollution, but they should not be confused with the rapporteur's proposal to reduce subsidies for fossil fuels as a sine qua non for the introduction of modern environmental protection solutions.
president-in-office of the council. mr president, this has been an interesting and stimulating debate, marked by almost total welcome – quite correctly – for mr wijkman’s report and for its contents, and by very real agreement on the nature and scale of the challenge. it has also been marked by a strong emphasis from many speakers on renewable resources, with various examples of this being cited, and also by strong differences of opinion over nuclear power. i would say to the last speaker, mrs harms, that if the only aspect of the climate change debate she heard in the uk was that of nuclear power, then she must have moved in very restricted circles, because there is a great deal being discussed in the uk, which has not actually made a fresh commitment to nuclear power, despite a commitment to discussing it. in fact, energy efficiency is top of the uk’s list of policies for tackling climate change, just as she would wish. there has been much emphasis on what are usually known in the jargon as ‘co-benefits’. some speakers emphasised the damage caused by air pollution by the same gases that are contributing to climate change, while others emphasised that, as we tackle climate change, we will derive other potential health benefits from the reduction in the use of those gases. mrs gutiérrez-cortines asked about the role of agriculture. as she may know, in countries such as new zealand, livestock are the source of almost all greenhouse gas emissions, making this a particularly difficult problem to solve. there is therefore no doubt that agriculture can, in certain circumstances, be part of the problem. however, as a number of speakers mentioned with regard to biomass and biofuels, it also could also be part of the solution. that is an issue that will come under increasing scrutiny. i am sorry mr hegyi is opposed to carbon capture and storage. the sad and blunt fact is that countries like india and china, which need to grow and develop in order to tackle poverty – and this was another issue referred to, again quite correctly, in the debate – have huge coal reserves and will use them, because they feel they have no choice. it is surely better for us to try to find ways of helping them to do that sustainably, through technologies like carbon capture and storage, rather than simply telling them not to use those power sources, which i fear would be fruitless. all the references made to the most vulnerable states and to the most vulnerable within other countries heighten the need for the actions the eu must take on adaptation, and support for adaptation, to impacts that we cannot avoid. strong emphasis has been placed on the role of the many other countries involved and on the need for a global dialogue – with which the council wholeheartedly agrees – and there is clear agreement both that the eu should continue to take the lead internationally and that we should continue to place strong emphasis on delivering on our own programmes. mrs doyle and mr hökmark both suggested that the eu is unlikely to meet its kyoto targets. that is not my understanding of the latest position as assessed by the commission. however, that is a report that we will be publishing as we approach montreal, and it certainly remains the case that we must continue to maintain and indeed step up our own activity. that brings me to the comments by both mrs lucas and mr smith, who quite rightly praised the ambition of the wijkman report in setting a target of a 60% reduction in emissions by 2050, without apparently being aware that this is the target the uk government set in its own energy white paper in 2003. perhaps, though, this should come as no a surprise, since mrs lucas had nothing good to say about the uk’s approach. however, i must put it firmly on the record for her and on behalf of this council that it is a waste of everybody’s time to demand that the eu deliver a formal mandate and a formal timetable in montreal. this body above all should recognise that the world of imperialism is at an end. we cannot just march into montreal and dictate to the rest of the world how they should conduct themselves and go about their business, not least when we are talking to some of the poorest and most vulnerable countries in the world whose priority, quite rightly, is development and feeding their populations. we will not act in this manner. if we are able to kindle a dialogue and spark a process in montreal, it will be a real and substantial achievement, just as it was a real and substantial achievement to elicit the language and secure the programme of action agreed at gleneagles. we all agree that we ought to be moving faster, but let us at least recognise the fact that we are making some progress. (applause)
member of the commission. i should like to thank everyone who has participated in this rich and important debate. the need to act urgently to tackle climate change was underlined by mr wijkman and others. i believe that the action taken and the series of new initiatives put forward by the commission since the adoption of its communication in february clearly demonstrate its determination to act in this area. the european union's first priority in montreal is to build broad international support for further action and obtain agreement on starting a formal process to discuss the shape of a future multilateral climate change regime. once the discussions get going, the european union will need to consider the right moment for putting forward its views on targets under such a future regime. targets have proven to be a very useful tool in environmental policy making. they provide our guidance to decision-makers in society. they are particularly useful for industry and the private sector when they have to take long-term investment decisions. targets will therefore remain a core element of any future climate change architecture. we need targets. as you will be aware, the european council of last march set down a pathway target of 15% to 30% of emissions reductions by 2020. however, the commission believes that the time has not yet come to set concrete targets for developed countries in montreal in december. that would only be done when we have more clarity on the progress of the negotiations on the post-2012 period. mr seeber has underlined that any future climate change regime will have to build on broad participation on all major emitters and that is of key importance if our cooperation is to be truly efficient. the commission and member states are working hard to promote deeper dialogue with the united states and developing countries. we have engaged in policy dialogue with the united states administration within the united nations framework agreement on climate change and within other fora and meetings, such as the joint climate change science and technology workshop. that covers concrete topics such as renewable energy, energy efficiency and carbon sequestration. the united states claims that is has a different approach to fighting climate change, based mainly on the research and development of new technologies. the difference between their approach and our approach is that they have seen an approximate 15% increase in carbon dioxide emissions while the european union of 25 has seen a considerable reduction compared with 1990 levels, and the 15 member countries under the kyoto regime obligations are 1.7% under the 1990 level. that is not enough, but we are sure that, by the end of our commitment period, we will be in compliance with our kyoto target. this is the difference between the two approaches. as regards developing countries, the european union has an open mind on how they should participate in future multilateral climate cooperation. it is clear that we cannot expect the same mandatory requirements as we do from developed countries. any commitment they take on will be based on the principle of common, but differentiated, responsibilities. china and other developing countries have contributed to the formation of the greenhouse phenomenon by a much smaller percentage than the developed countries, and per capita emissions in china are currently less than one tenth of the levels in the developed world, so we should follow that example. where capita income is much lower and development needs greater we have to follow what the united nations convention wisely prescribes as a common but differentiated policy. mr verges mentioned that we should take particular care of developing countries and their increasing needs arising from global warming. we really should prepare for that impact. the commission is already providing funding and welcomes canada's intention to prepare a five-year work programme on adaptation at the conference in montreal. in addition, the european union is the major contributor to the 2001 bonn political declaration which pledges usd 410 million per year in climate change funding for developing countries, starting this year. at the october environment council, ministers committed themselves to communicating at montreal the progress being made towards delivery on this target. also, to support developing countries, we have to make sure that the clean development mechanisms actually work. the key issue is the efficiency of the executive board in bonn, and the european union is already providing funding, but more support is clearly necessary. the european union is still the main contributor of funds to the executive board. there have been certain concerns about bilateral cooperation outside the united nations context, and especially in the asia-pacific partnership. let me stress that this can in no way be viewed as an alternative to the united nations process. however, this partnership can support our efforts under the climate change convention and the kyoto protocol through closer bilateral cooperation that includes both a stronger political dialogue and a focus on technology. this is also how one should see the european union-china and european union-india partnerships. this translates into very concrete actions: we have recently held two workshops in india and china on the clean development mechanism and market-based mechanisms. in relation to china, we also see an important focus on the development and demonstration of near-zero emissions power generation, and i agree with mrs beckett that carbon capture and storage is one of the means of tackling the problem of climate change. it is not a cure-all, but it is one of the many means that we can use. these partnerships will have the positive and immediate effect of supporting the discussions on a multilateral climate change regime post-2012. mr blokland asked about the efficiency of the european union's current measures. if we implement all the measures in full, this will lead to a 4% reduction compared with 1990, which obviously is not sufficient to meet the target of -8% that we have set for ourselves. that is why we included additional measures in the climate change programme that we launched a month ago. this implies that we should make greater emission cuts, allowing us to reach the kyoto target and make further progress for the period after 2012. it is important to know that, for the european union of 25, the result with the existing measures will be -7%. mrs doyle, mrs grossetête and others asked about emissions from cars. i fully agree that this is a vital issue and that is why, in 2006, the commission will review the agreement with the car industry in order to assess the possibility of reaching the community objective of 120 g/km by a certain point, having made sure, of course, that we reach the target, voluntarily agreed with the car industry in europe, japan and korea, of 140 mg. mrs ek referred to the inclusion of transport in european union emissions trading. the commission has already made a proposal with regard to aviation, as you know. the commission will assess this for the other transport sectors as part of the 2006 review. on renewable energy, the commission will put forward, in the weeks to come, a new report assessing a target for renewable energy by 2020. regarding nuclear energy and the remarks made by mr hökmark, some member states expect nuclear energy to be a part of their future energy. however, we have to ensure that we have a broad range of energy sources that are low in carbon. nuclear power will not be able to meet the increased energy demands and we should also be aware that nuclear power faces problems concerning nuclear waste and public opinion. with regard to what mrs gutiérrez-cortines said about agriculture, the commission agrees that synergies can be found between climate change and agriculture. we had an extremely interesting meeting in london, organised by mrs beckett and the uk presidency, on climate change and agriculture and very important conclusions were reached there. the commission will be putting forward a plan in support of biofuels. finally, winning the battle against climate change requires determined action, starting now. it requires action, as mr smith said, from all actors and sectors of society. we should not underestimate the size of the challenge. winning the battle against climate change will take time, of which we have precious little, and efforts that some will argue we cannot afford. with your continued support, we are determined to reassert the european union's leadership in this key challenge for mankind. thank you very much.

responsible for almost 60% of development aid, systematically spreads its aid through 26 different programming documents and implements this aid through 26 different procedures? i think not. it's not acceptable. europe's influence and effectiveness must be commensurate with its means, and that is precisely why i have proposed to the member states and to the european parliament a common foundation for the whole of the european union, a foundation which brings together its values, its objectives, its principles and its scope of action, and which applies to the whole of the european union. this foundation, the european consensus, would be an indispensable step towards more coordinated, complementary and resolute action by the european union. what's this about? we, parliament, the council and the commission, share the same values which are the founding values of the union. we share a common goal: to eradicate poverty wherever it exists. we share an international agenda: the millennium development goals and the millennium declaration. we share principles of partnership: shared responsibility between industrialized and developing countries, ownership of poverty reduction strategies by partner countries, participation of civil society and non-state actors. we share the principles of aid effectiveness: concentration so as not to fragment efforts, policy coherence, coordination and division of labour between donors, harmonisation of our procedures, alignment with the strategies of partner countries. the motion for a resolution which mr wijkman is presenting today is remarkable. it highlights the main positive elements of the commission's communication and it contributes constructively to improving consensus, which has helped us a lot in our tripartite discussions, and i thank it for that. i congratulate him and your parliament on this contribution of exceptional quality. i should like to sum up briefly the points of the resolution which i support wholeheartedly, the points which are the basis of our consensus. firstly, a clear reference to the declaration on development policy in the regulation which will govern the financial instrument for development cooperation. this response will no doubt strengthen the very status of the declaration. secondly, the analysis of poverty as a multidimensional phenomenon, which requires a range of responses and a balance between the socioeconomic and environmental pillars of sustainable development. thirdly, the importance of equality between men and women. i should like to inform you that the commission has proposed that parliament's text be included among the guiding principles of the declaration. fourth, the approach is rights-based. i believe that the commission's proposal to include human rights and good governance as complementary objectives to poverty reduction is a perfect response to parliament's request. fifthly, all the priorities mentioned in the resolution are covered by the community's areas of action: the prevention and treatment of aids and other diseases, reproductive health, gender equality, adaptation to climate change, trade for development, conflict prevention, good governance, the fight against corruption, the promotion of decent work, including the fight against child labour. and finally, we welcome the fact that parliament is open to moving towards budget support, because it allows countries to be efficient and develop their capacities. in this way we can support improved public financial management and support the institutions, including national parliaments. these institutions must play their full role and act as guardians of budgets. at the same time, i am convinced that it is a powerful means of initiating and nurturing political dialogue with our partners. i therefore thank parliament for making a significant contribution to more effective action for development through this resolution, which lays the foundation for our good cooperation in the future.

amendment concerns a restriction on the level of the standard rate by setting a maximum level of 25% to prevent growing divergence in the standard rates of vat applied by the member states. this would require a new proposal from the commission, thus preventing the adoption on time of a minimum rate to be applied as from 1 january 2006. moreover, given past experience it has no chance of being unanimously adopted by the council. the second amendment aims at allowing more flexibility in vat provisions in order to enable member states to react to the changing economic situation. this is not in line with the first amendment, which tries precisely to prevent such flexibility as regards the standard rate. generally speaking, this proposal is not yet the appropriate vehicle for carrying out taxable person to hand in the requested additional information. the amendment is, furthermore, in contradiction with the second subparagraph of the same article, which mentions that a new period of three months starts to run as from the moment the additional information is received from the taxable person. i am convinced that the positive opinion of parliament will contribute to a timely experimental arrangements is not really a viable way forward. moreover, we need to be very cautious, since a unanimous agreement in the council on such an extension would seem as hard to achieve as a
