mr. chairman, please! ladies and gentlemen! i would like to thank mr blokland and to stress the importance of the batteries and accumulators directive and the waste batteries and accumulators directive for the protection of the environment. studies have been conducted on people living in ecological areas and water sources, and in many cases metals similar to those used in batteries and accumulators have been found. analysis of the origin of these metals suggests that they came from, among other things, batteries and accumulators that were thrown away in landfills. the decay time of discarded batteries and accumulators is very long. there are several problems, such as: underestimating the need and collection of batteries, the problem of popularizing the need for their collection and creating legal and financial means to support these activities, the problem of developing a culture and habit of collecting this waste in society, the problem of organizing and disposing of this pollution. a number of issues raised require time and continuous publicity, as well as improvements in the collection and disposal system. it also requires the promotion of technical progress in the development of their production, in particular, in order to ensure the safety of batteries.
member of the commission. mr president, i will focus now only the amendments relating to three key issues in this file: firstly, the legal basis; secondly, the definitions of ‘portable’ and ‘industrial’ battery types and, thirdly, collection targets. firstly, on the legal basis, the preamble and recital 1 – amendments 1 and 2: the commission continues to support the concept of a dual legal basis for this directive as the correct one. this dual legal basis reflects the dual objective of the proposed directive. indeed, the directive aims at achieving both a high level of environmental protection and contributing to the proper functioning of the internal market. moreover, it should be noted that the proposed directive specifies that each individual article has only one legal basis. indeed, the articles laying down provisions for the environmental protection are based on article 175 of the ec treaty. the articles laying down provisions related to the proper functioning of the internal market – namely articles 4, 5 and 18 of the proposed directive – are based on article 95 of the treaty. consequently, this dual legal basis cannot lead to any legal incompatibilities of procedures. secondly, on the definition of the different battery types – articles 3(3) and (6) and recitals 8 and 9, amendments 5, 6, 12 and 13: the definitions of ‘portable’ batteries and ‘industrial’ batteries are important since they determine the scope of the cadmium ban and the type of collection requirements. therefore, the commission is of the opinion that definitions should meet the following criteria: they should be clear, they should be workable in practice for the member states to implement in a harmonised way, and any overlaps or gaps should be avoided. taking into account the above, the commission supports the first two parts of amendment 12, in particular the introduction of the weight limit for defining portable batteries. however, the commission does not support the other changes proposed to the definitions of the different battery types – amendment 12, third part, and amendment 13. the commission welcomes the deletion of the non-exhaustive list of examples in the recitals, which considerably improves the drafting of the legislative act. thirdly, i turn to the collection targets – article 9(2) and (4) and amendments 26 to 28. the commission believes that setting collection targets in the proposed directive is necessary: firstly to ensure a minimum level of environmental protection in all member states and secondly to monitor the efficiency of the national battery-collection schemes. it is important that the collection targets are ambitious in environmental terms, but they should also be achievable, realistic and cost-efficient. the commission’s extended impact assessment carefully analysed this issue and came to the conclusion that the collection target of 160 grams or 40% would be the most cost-efficient target, which corresponds with part of amendment 26. the appropriateness of an increase in the target in the longer term will be carefully reviewed, as foreseen in article 20(2)(b) of the proposed directive. in this review, the commission will take account of technical progress and practical experience gained in member states. the commission thus in principle supports amendment 26 but reserves its opinion on amendment 56. the commission supports the amendment which deletes the possibility for member states to derogate from the proposed collection targets – the ‘transitional arrangements’. the commission had proposed this possibility since, in its initial proposal, the collection targets were based on weight per inhabitant. since the collection targets are now based on sales, it is no longer necessary to provide for this possibility of transitional arrangements. since the proposed directive already foresees a review of the long-term targets in article 20(2)(b), the commission does not see the need for a specific review obligation to increase the targets by a specific date. i will give a voting list to the secretariat, indicating which amendments are and are not acceptable to the commission. i should like to point out that the commission reserves its opinion on the additional 18 amendments tabled before the plenary, since more time is needed to fully assess the environmental, economic and social impacts thereof. i believe that the european parliament and the council can now start moving towards agreement on this file. i look forward to an early conclusion of the codecision process so that the directive can be implemented by the member states and we can achieve a high level of environmental protection in this area.

in writing. among the environmental provisions negotiated in the accession treaties was the previous directive 91/157/eec setting the levels of recovery and disposal of batteries. the european commission is now proposing a new system for the collection, treatment and disposal of waste batteries and accumulators. poland has transposed the provisions of the previous directive into national law and we are now in the implementation phase. suddenly, new solutions are proposed and collection levels are set much higher than before. this is certainly the right way to ensure safety and to improve the environmental quality of europe, but it must be done in a way that is consistent with existing solutions. unfortunately, most of the amendments of the rapporteur are not supported by any studies and assessment of the impact on the development of companies in this sector. and it is the entrepreneurs who will bear the costs of the new law. the collection levels proposed in amendments nos 26 and 27 are requirements which are impossible for most member states to meet. the new member states are only in the process of establishing a complex system for the collection of waste batteries based on the directive. there's no rational explanation today for the 40 percent and 60 percent collection levels. the proposal to increase the recycling rate to 55% is also unacceptable and unjustified. moreover, an efficient battery collection system is linked to the promotion and development of social habits, which requires a long-term approach when proposing new solutions.

president-in-office of the council. the council has on several occasions noted the possible benefits of an agreement on further changes in the world trade organization’s outcomes during negotiations in the framework of the doha development agenda within the wto. the council has expressed support for future comprehensive multilateral negotiations, which reflects its wish for substantial progress in world trade liberalisation, securing continuing global economic growth, increased job creation, prosperity and sustainable development, and addressing the concerns of civil society. the council has noted that a further multilateral change of trade was the best way to meet the challenges posed by economic and technological change and increasing globalisation. the council sees this multilateral change as the most appropriate approach for achieving substantial and balanced results for the benefit of all wto members. a number of studies have tried to assess the magnitude of the benefits for the european union. for example, a widely-cited world bank study in 2005 estimates that the potential gains from full liberalisation of global merchandise trade would be around usd 65 billion for the eu-25 and the efta countries by 2015. the council has not explicitly commented on the consequences ‘if no deal is done’. the ramifications of a failed round go much wider than trade. it would send a negative message about multilateral cooperation. on the contrary, a good trade deal is an important part of our efforts to tackle poverty and promote global security in the long term, which have been such a focus of our work in the course of our presidency.

in writing. as someone who has worked with the disabled community for many years, i offer the following reasoning. disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility due to disability or other conditions, such as old age, remain full citizens even during the journey. this group of persons includes blind and deaf-mutes who require appropriate access to information while travelling. it is wrong to charge disabled people for additional air travel. it is suggested that these costs (not so high) be included in the general costs of the individual carriers. disabled people should be guaranteed that their needs will be met throughout the union, regardless of the airline or airport they use. assistance should be provided at every stage of the journey (moving around the terminal, provision of a wheelchair and a carer at the check-in desk, boarding and disembarking, baggage collection, transfer, etc.). it is advisable to ask carriers to install appropriate facilities to facilitate the boarding and disembarkation of disabled persons. passenger aircraft designers should also take care to adapt the width of aisles, the size of toilets, etc., to the needs of persons with reduced mobility. there is also a need to harmonise the disability assistance system in union air transport, including the establishment of a service standard applicable to all community airports.

, on behalf of the pse group . mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i would like to draw attention to the dangerous tendency in russia of president putin's system to use the prosecution and the judiciary for political struggle. on december 9 this year, russian prosecutors charged the bank nieftianoj with money laundering and tax fraud. the bank's board is headed by boris nemtsov, one of russia's most accomplished liberal politicians, who has played a key role in building the opposition to president putin, especially in the run-up to the upcoming 2008 presidential elections, which will determine the future course of democracy in russia. boris nemtsov, in a speech to a newsletter published by my parliamentary office in november of this year, speaks of the danger of building state-monopoly capitalism in russia and sees the process now, i quote, of "russian lukashenko". the european union should abolish the requirement for russians to have visas to enter the countries of the union. the abolition of visas is a guarantee for russian civil society to democratize russia.
mr. chairman, please! it is a pity that we are discussing the issue of human rights violations in russia on thursday afternoon, when we are devoting a lot of time to tunisia - in the plenary of parliament and with the media - on wednesday. one of the fundamental values of the european union, which is the basis of democracy, is freedom of speech and thought. this is reflected in the activities of hundreds of thousands of ngos, which are the third most powerful force in europe. unfortunately, we are witnessing the introduction of laws in russia that are foreign and incomprehensible to us europeans. russia is moving further and further away from democratic standards, and we cannot stand by and watch the basic rights being curtailed in a country that has the status of a privileged state. we cannot be indifferent to the blatantly anti-democratic changes. access to foreign funds for russian ngos will be hampered or even prevented. the new restrictions are expected to affect as many as 450,000 organizations in russia. the russian federation has adopted measures to restrict the participation of foreign companies in the russian federation. the new law prohibits the activities of branches of representative offices of international and foreign organizations in russia on the existing basis. this means that they will have to close their existing branches and apply for a new organisation independent of their parent. foreigners who are not permanently registered in russia will lose the right to form social organizations and will not have the right to sit on their boards or be their members. the arguments of some russian politicians that ngos are a tool of third countries in their foreign policy towards russia are absurd and ridiculous to the democratic system. this attitude is condemned and strongly opposed by the european union, and is a manifestation of the growing xenophobia among russia's political elites. the number of 450 000 ngos in russia and their activity testify to the popularity of this sphere of public and social life in russia. the european union should support this manifestation of civil society.
mr. chairman, please! i wish that these merry christmas wishes would reach the ethiopians, although i think for many of them it will be a sad christmas. i say this because ethiopia, one of the two largest countries in africa, is also a largely christian country, with christian roots. i think this is one of the additional reasons why a number of countries of the european union, also of christian origin, should defend human rights in this country. i hope that the commissioner will not today be like an african animal, an ostrich that hides its head in the sand, that he will speak boldly about the will and determination of the european commission, the authorities of the european union, to stand up for human rights in a country where they are, of course, violated. with such faith in you, commissioner, i hope and the whole house, i wish you a merry christmas too.
